#920. Man United set to appeal Leny Yoro’s red card against Liverpool after Bruno Fernandes’ referee rant

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Leny Yoro was sent off inside the opening 10 minutes of Mauricio Pochettino’s first game in charge of Manchester United

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Manchester United are set to appeal the red card handed to Leny Yoro during their 4-0 defeat against Liverpool at Anfield on Sunday.

The defender was sent off just eight minutes into the contest after being penalised for a challenge on Liverpool forward Alexander Isak as the Swedish international ran through towards goal.

Referee Sam Barrott deemed that Yoro had denied an obvious goalscoring opportunity, despite Isak appearing to have lost control of the ball prior to the tackle.

Dominik Szoboszlai scored from the subsequent free-kick to put Liverpool ahead, with the hosts then going on to pick a comfortable victory that marked a dismal start to Mauricio Pochettino’s tenure as United’s new head coach.

It is understood that United now plan to lodge an official appeal in the hope of having Yoro’s suspension overturned.

Speaking to the BBC following the final whistle, United captain Bruno Fernandes insisted it was "never a red card", adding: "I think it’s too many referees on the pitch and too many on VAR, seated, with such a long time to see and put it back, go forward, put it back, do it in slow motion, whatsoever.

"To make a mistake like this can change a game. But obviously, then, it’s not because of them that we concede the goal from the free-kick, but it changes completely the flow of the game."

United currently sit 19th in the Premier League table after suffering their fifth defeat of the season on Sunday. They have only won one of their 11 league games to date - a 5-2 victory over Ipswich Town in August.

Following Szoboszlai’s free-kick, Florian Wirtz doubled Liverpool’s lead within two minutes to give United a huge mountain to climb.

Pochettino opted to bring Harry Maguire on for Bryan Mbeumo to try and tighten things up at the back after Yoro’s dismissal, but Liverpool continued to create chance after chance.

They were eventually rewarded when Rio Ngumoha made it 3-0 in the 66th minute, before substitute Victor Munoz completed the rout eight minutes from time.

Liverpool return to Champions League action against Club Brugge on Wednesday, while United also play on the same day against Sporting Lisbon.

#919. Norway's ice hockey team says Russia replacing it at World Juniors

The wrangling over Russia's return to international ice hockey continues, with Norway saying it has been kicked out of the next major tournament to accommodate Russia. Switzerland has joined a "boycott."

With just weeks to go until the start of the 2027 World Junior Championship, it remains unclear who will be the 10th, and final, participant. This comes after the Norwegian Ice Hockey Association said the International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) had said it had been removed from the tournament so that Russia could take part.

The move, which has yet to be publicly announced by the IIHF, comes in apparent response to the Court of Arbitration (CAS) ruling in late October, which ordered it to allow Russia to return to international play. The World Juniors is the first tournament affected by the CAS decision.

The IIHF barred Russia and Belarus from international play shortly after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

In a statement issued Saturday, the IIHF said it was "taking the necessary steps required by the CAS ruling and reviewing what conditions would need to be met to safeguard our Championships, protect the organization's financial stability and secure the long-term future of international ice hockey."

As of Monday, the IIHF website still listed Norway as one of the participants in the World Juniors, which is to be hosted by Edmonton and Red Deer, Alberta, beginning on December 26. But Swiss Ice Hockey has responded to Norway's statement, saying its team would not face Russia at the World Juniors — as would be the case if it replaces Norway in the schedule.

However, it's far from certain that Russia will actually be able to ice a team in the tournament, as just last week, the Canadian prime minister ruled out the possibility.

"While Russia and Belarus are supporting this illegal, unjustified ​war in Ukraine, as long as that's going on, there will be none of those athletes competing for their countries in Canada," said Mark Carney.

"So, ​if you're asking specifically about the World Juniors, the Russians will not be there."

How this circle could be squared is unclear. Carney's pledge, coupled with the stated refusal by Finland, Sweden, Switzerland and others to face Russia in an international tournament, appears to have given the Norwegian Ice Hockey Association (NIHF) hope that its team could still play in the upcoming tournament. Several long-time corporate sponsors have also threatened to pull out if Russia is allowed to compete.

"This makes us hope that the last word has not been said about our participation in Canada in December," said NIHF General Secretary Petter Salsten.

"The Norwegian Ice Hockey Association is awaiting further information from the IIHF in the coming days."

Meanwhile, the German Ice Hockey Association (DEB) is still in discussions with the government in Berlin and the IIHF about how to proceed — or not — with hosting the Men's Ice Hockey World Championship in May.

"We intend to host the world championship in Germany next year, and I am very optimistic that we will succeed in doing so," DEB chairman Frank H. Lutz told German broadcaster MagentaSport on Saturday.

While he acknowledged the IIHF's CAS-ordered requirement to include Russia and reiterated the DEB's rejection of the court ruling, he provided no indication as to how this obstacle could be overcome.

Lutz, who said he would be in Berlin for more consultations this week, had previously said handing back Germany's hosting rights was a possibility — if only as a last resort.

On Friday, government spokesman Stefan Kornelius said Berlin supports the DEB's efforts to find a solution.

"However, given the boycotts that would follow Russia's readmission, that would effectively be impossible. For this reason, we intend to explore, through dialogue, how we can still ensure the tournament takes place."

Asked at the same press conference whether Germany could issue visas to a Russian team for the tournament, a Foreign Ministry spokesman indicated that this would be difficult under restrictions currently in place.

"At a time when Russia is waging a war of aggression against Ukraine, there can be no 'normalcy' — and we will certainly not pretend that there is," said spokesperson Martin Giese.

However, he did not categorically rule out the possibility.

It has been suggested that government officials could be choosing their words carefully out of concern for Munich's chances as it bids to host the Summer Olympics in 2036, 2040 or 2044.

The International Olympic Committee (IOC) recently lifted its sanctions on Russian athletes and suspension of the Russian National Olympic Committee, opening the door for their return to competition despite the ongoing war in Ukraine.

The thinking goes that the IOC would expect national Olympic committees who are bidding to host an Olympic Games — like the German Olympic Sports Confederation (DOSB) — to follow its lead.

Asked whether the debate over Russia's possible involvement in a hockey tournament could affect Munich's chances, government spokesman Kornelius said he didn't wish to "speculate on implications."

Still, with the IOC set to decide in the next few weeks whether Munich advances to the next stage of the process, one has to think that the issue could hardly have come up at a more inopportune time for the DOSB.

#917. Any regrets, Mauricio? Man Utd are deep in relegation battle after Anfield farce

The Liverpool fans did not miss a beat. They never do. “Poch is at the wheel,” they goaded as this calamity unfolded. But at the wheel of what, a clown car? The look of thunder on Mauricio Pochettino’s face said it all as he got off to the worst start of any Manchester United manager – or head coach – in 100 years.

The Pochettino bandwagon rolled into town with the usual fanfare of a new era, new belief, new hope; and then the wheels came off, the doors collapsed and the engine exploded. The opening quarter of an hour really was that farcical.

In that time, away to Liverpool of all places, they were 2-0 down, a player down – and down and out. If Pochettino had any uncertainty over the scale of the task ahead of him, there it was laid bare. Of course United had some mitigation. They played almost the entire game with 10 men, but teams have coped with that before and shown far more resistance and resilience. By the time United did that, it was game over. No one expected a quick fix, but come on.

Any regrets, Mauricio? Whatever the salary, he could be forgiven for having a few as he watched on. This is a far cry from being in charge of the United States and watching them roll over Haiti 8-0 on aggregate, as he did last week. If Liverpool had been more ruthless, it could have been 8-0 here.

In the end it was 4-0 – the same scoreline by which Lal Hilditch lost his first game at United, away to Bolton Wanderers in October 1926. Hilditch was a stop-gap player-manager and former central defender Pochettino may well have been tempted to bring himself on, even at the age of 54. He could barely have done worse.

Pochettino, too, can take some responsibility. Eyebrows were certainly raised when he dropped Harry Maguire – who he then had to bring on after 22 minutes – to hand Matthijs de Ligt his first Premier League start in 357 days. De Ligt was then at fault for the first and, arguably, the second goal.

Did the head coach start with a back three or a back four? The players seemed confused. It eventually ended up as a back five.

But this was a collective failing for United. From the top – with director of football Jason Wilcox caught on camera with his head buried in his coat – through the club and out on the pitch. Pochettino is big on building a culture. So he has to abolish the comedy and the chaos and restore credibility.

United are deep in a relegation battle. Have no doubt. Eight points after 11 games means they are currently on target for fewer than 28 points, which is a lower points-per-game total than when they were relegated in 1974.

The work needed at United is monumental. The transfer strategy has been inexplicable, with the decision being to rebuild the attack last year, the midfield this summer and wait until next year to remodel the defence. The folly of that has been exposed by the fact that United have conceded 34 goals already this season, the most in the top five European leagues.

United will argue, with justification, that Leny Yoro’s eighth-minute sending-off for denial of a goalscoring opportunity was harsh given that Alexander Isak appeared to have already lost control of the ball. But what was Yoro thinking as he bundled into the back of the forward? And what was De Ligt doing as he watched on, or lumbered on, after failing to track the run from Ronald Araújo’s ball over the top?

Leny Yoro is SENT OFF after eight minutes! 😱 https://t.co/VKYvckvBBP

The second goal highlighted that mismatch as Rio Ngumoha easily beat Diogo Dalot, not for the first or last time, and pulled back a cross that Florian Wirtz hooked in off the crossbar. De Ligt was all over the place as he again watched on.

It can be argued that, after that calamitous start, Pochettino stemmed the bleeding just as it appeared set to be a bloodbath. But that may also have owed much to a lack of killer instinct from Liverpool, who did not go for the jugular.

Liverpool bulldoze the 10-man visitors to earn an emphatic 4-0 victory. Pochettino’s first game in charge of Man Utd ends in a heavy and disappointing defeat. This result moves the hosts up to fourth, while Man Utd are floundering in 19th, with just one win and 23 goals conceded in 11 league matches.

Man Utd fly forward on the counter through Zirkzee, who has Fernandes running up in support. Zirkzee finds the Man Utd captain and he forces Alisson into a late save. There are ironic cheers as the Liverpool goalkeeper is finally called into action. He looks destined to end this game with a clean sheet.

There will be two minutes of added time before this Man Utd nightmare is over.

It goes from bad to worse for Man Utd... De Ligt’s poor clearance only goes as far as Van Dijk and Liverpool recycle the ball. Liverpool will eye a fifth to further embarrass their bitter rivals.

What a goal from Víctor Muñoz to make it 4-0 to Liverpool against Manchester United! ☄️ https://t.co/x7G78ccrMa

The away end is starting to empty, as they have seen enough. The thing that should worry them is the fact that derision is raining down on their team, that everyone knows they are a laughing stock. Mauricio Pochettino is being serenaded - if that is the right phrase - with a chorus of “Poch is at the wheel!”, a sense that even he won’t stop this tanker from running aground.

Ngumoha departs to a standing ovation from the Anfield crowd as he replaced by Frimpong, who makes his return from injury. The young winger has been one of the standout performers for Liverpool today and has torn Man Utd’s defence apart at times.

It’s wave after wave of Liverpool pressure. The home side fly forward on the counter through Wirtz, who tees up Isak. The striker chops inside and forces Lammens into a strong save. Moments later, Szoboszlai draws another stop from the Man Utd goalkeeper with yet another long-range effort. For the third time in a minute, the hosts go close once again, with Van Dijk flicking Wirtz’s searching delivery just wide.

Iraola turns to his bench for the first time today and orders a double change, with Nyoni and Munoz replacing Mac Allister and Barcola.

Liverpool are close to a fourth as Wirtz turns away from Mainoo and plays in Barcola, who is denied by Martinez’s last-ditch block.

That is Barcola at his devastating best. The Frenchman breezes past a non-existent Martinez on the halfway line and unselfishly slides the ball across goal for Ngumoha, who coolly powers a close-range effort under Lammens to all but seal the victory. Barcola carved Man Utd apart and Ngumoha showcased unerring composure. It’s a wonderfully worked goal.

Rio Ngumoha finishes off a CLINICAL counter-attack for Liverpool! 😮‍💨 https://t.co/SaNQv6o4AZ

Barcola turns his marker and clips an effort over the bar. Pochettino makes a double change as Mount and Mazraoui replace Tielemans and Dorgu.

Isak wastes a golden chance! De Ligt stretches to intercepts Wirtz’s pass and completely misses the ball. Isak latches onto the mistake and is through on goal, but from a tight angle, he wildly slices a powerful shot wide. You expect so much more from the Liverpool striker there.

Barcola catches Tielemans with a late challenge as the Man Utd midfielder goes to clear and picks up a yellow card.

Now there’s something interesting. The Kop has chanted in unison during that little break in play: “Attack! Attack! Attack, attack, attack!” They know their team has dropped down the gears and they want to be careful it doesn’t prove costly.

Wirtz slips a piercing pass in behind Man Utd’s defence for Barcola. However, the unmarked Frenchman lacks composure as he attempts to round Lammens and takes a poor touch, with the ball bobbling out of play. Barcola has caused Man Utd a lot of problems but has notably lacked end-product.

Jacquet beats Fernandes to Mainoo’s through ball thanks to the defender’s blistering pace. Fernandes trips Jacquet and the referee sounds his whistle.

In fairness to Man Utd, since Maguire’s 22nd-minute introduction, they’ve limited Liverpool to very few attacking openings, despite the hosts’ numerical advantage.

The chatter during the interval with some esteemed former Liverpool players was that the current team need to be a little more ruthless, as opposed to trying to walk the ball into the net. Mauricio Pochettino has, in fairness, shown that he can stop the bleeding but, for Liverpool, the onus is on them to demolish United. If they don’t get a third goal soon, it’s curious to say but the stadium will feel edgy.

Bruno Fernandes says he has shelved talks over a new contract because it is not the “right moment” for discussions over his future as Manchester United captain.

Fernandes, 32, is out of contract next summer although United have a 12-month option to extend his deal to 2028.

The Portugal midfielder is understood to have rejected two contract offers from United since the summer but said all his focus needs to be on trying to help the team out of their current plight.

United head into Sunday’s game against Liverpool at Anfield second from bottom in the Premier League.

“We spoke about the contract at the end of last season,” Fernandes told Sky Sports.

“We came in at the beginning of this season speaking about the contract, but about the context of the team and the club, I just put that to a side because I don’t think it’s the right moment, neither for me, nor for the club, to be talking about negotiations.

“The most important thing now is that the club gets back to winning games.”

Fernandes said claims he wants more money or a longer-term deal on offer are incorrect and that if finances were the issue he would have left Old Trafford before now. The captain has previously rejected lucrative offers from Saudi Arabia.

“The club offered me a new contract, so I think that, from their side, shows that they want me to stay,” he said.

“There’s no negotiations ongoing, but I’ve seen people saying that ‘He’s asked for more money, he’s asked for more years’. If I wanted more money, I wouldn’t be here.

“I had somewhere to go to get much more money than being at Manchester United. I could have been in a place that is much warmer than Manchester.

“Two summers ago, three summers ago, last summer, I always had the chance to leave and I always chose to be here.

“The thing is, I’ve always showed how much I care about the club and how much I want to win at this club. And I always said, in the moment the club thinks it’s time for me to move on, I will move on.

“I’m not going to be the player that I’ve seen many in this time at Manchester United. They’re going to stay here just by staying, just finish my contract and then we will see. In the moment the club says, ‘Bruno, it’s time to part ways’, I’m going to be the first one walking out the door.”

United chief executive Omar Berrada said of Fernandes on Friday that it was “true that we’re having conversations about his new contract” but that the club preferred “to keep that private”.

Having been voted PFA Player of the Year last season, Fernandes’ form has dropped off this term like that of the team.

He was dropped for the 3-0 defeat by Bournemouth in the wake of a 4-1 drubbing by Como when he criticised the tactics and approach of then head coach Michael Carrick.

Mauricio Pochettino, Carrick’s successor, confirmed on Friday that Fernandes would remain as captain.

Fernandes said the United fans had been “far too patient with us” and hopes Pochettino - who wanted to bring the Portuguese to Spurs in 2019 - will bring a fresh energy.

“He’s someone that likes to bring a very good energy to the team, someone very positive, very strong, strict, said it straight away that he won’t allow us to not give him what he demands from the team, from each player,” Fernandes said.

“He wants the club to succeed so much, he wants to win games, and that’s pretty clear and obvious by the way he and his staff speak and want us to improve.

“Obviously [in 2019] I was a very young player that was eager to come to the Premier League. They had [Harry] Kane there, they had Dele Alli, Son, the chance of playing with those players in front was very attractive.”

Mauricio Pochettino has outlined his vision of changing the culture at Manchester United in his attempt to lift the club out of the Premier League relegation zone.

Pochettino arrived in the country on Wednesday after his final matches in charge of the US national team. He has inherited a squad with some players who have publicly criticised their own coach and technical director this season during their slide down the table.

The new United head coach, who has a contract until 2029, mentioned “culture” seven times in his first club interview in a pointed analysis of the work he needs to do at Old Trafford, starting with this weekend’s match against Liverpool at Anfield.

“The culture, to create the culture is the most important,” Pochettino said. “To have the culture is the most important. Create the habit, the principle and I think that is what we want to create. We need to look forward and to find a way to create the best habit and the culture that makes us to be close to win every single game.”

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of the game everyone has been waiting for as Manchester United prepare to face Liverpool at Anfield in Mauricio Pochettino’s first outing in charge of the club.

Quiet international break at Man Utd? Don’t be ridiculous. Following a dismal start to the season, which has left today’s visitors 19th in the league table with just one win from 10 matches, Michael Carrick was eventually relieved of his duties as head coach and replaced by Pochettino, who left his role as the United States head coach after two years at the helm.

Pochettino has been handed the unenviable task of attempting to rescue Man Utd’s desperate situation in an extremely tumultuous time for the club under the co-ownership of the Glazers and Sir Jim Ratcliffe.

“I think what we need to do is to be very open-minded and try to do our best to try to perform and the players need to buy the idea of we need to improve, and that is our job. #916. The dangerous gamble Man United face in bid to escape a brutal reality

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Man United’s squad building has become a vicious cycle, writes Miguel Delaney, with Mauricio Pochettino already facing a crunch decision to salvage a nightmare season

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

After wrestling with one season-defining dilemma for weeks, the Manchester United hierarchy might immediately face another following their latest humiliation at the hands of bitter rivals Liverpool. Do they spend the £150m they can just about get away with in a difficult January window, affecting future planning, or actually risk a future that is almost unimaginable: relegation.

The weight of that decision is only made heavier by a much more difficult decision facing Mauricio Pochettino.

What system does he go with? What approach can actually amplify the abilities of these players? What formation can get them out of this mess, and just steady things?

Ideally, Pochettino would play his high-pressing system in a 4-3-3… but we’re a long way from ideals. We're into brutal realities. This squad just isn’t ready for that, and the manager faces yet another dilemma in how trying to prepare them for such an approach might bring a brutal learning period that only worsens an already dismal situation. They don’t have that luxury right now.

Can Pochettino do something similar to what Antonio Conte did with Chelsea in 2016-17 and tailor a formation to fit, or is that even possible? One insider tells the Independent about yet another contradiction in its strange construction. They were bemoaning the quality of the centre-halves, one of the few areas where the squad is overstocked, but pointed to how the latter almost dictates that you have to lean on them.

The urgency of the situation almost warrants Pochettino just going to a back five in a bid to grind out a few badly-needed wins.

In other words, break glass for emergency.

But then that’s where they are, an emergency; an extreme situation that has incrementally been arrived at.

It’s a bit like bankruptcy, an analogy that is by this point at bit too fitting: gradually then all at once.

The state of the squad is a manifestation of all of that.

As recently as five years ago, United were paying out one of the highest wage bills in football. Not all of that expenditure may have been worth it but the sheer expense offered a certain insulation.

That insulation has frayed to the point of vanishing.

The club’s financial situation, as they seek to service so much debt, has influenced and combined with the team’s lack of success to force their level - in quality and spending power - further and further down.

It didn’t help that, throughout that time, the squad was constantly dragged this way and that depending on the demands of different managers.

So they are left with this, and a situation where no one in European football agrees with chief executive Omar Berrada’s comments that they have “made the squad fundamentally better”.

The chief executive of another recent Champions League club instead tells the Independent that United have “an incredibly poorly constructed squad”.

Another experienced football figure says it is “damning” on INEOS’ running of football operations, especially since their supposedly enlightened decisions seem to have made things worse.

This is almost the greater frustration with this leadership. It is as if they didn’t quite grasp what they were taking over.

Because, in a certain context, some of the signings obviously make sense. United specifically wanted to get away from this problem of buying players to certain managerial approaches, so instead went for “adaptability” in talent like Matheus Cunha and Bryan Mbuemo.

But that adaptability only works properly if you know what you are adapting from; if there is a core idea that such signings can work around. United’s most major recent additions instead look like cosmetic additions, rather than the surgery this squad really needs.

Again, they point to that core that has been there for so long, almost the opposite of Chelsea’s problems.

It is not that they are individually bad players, despite increasing and understandable excoriation from the stands.

It is that they have all been there too long, carrying too much “scar tissue” - something said a lot about Tottenham Hotspur last season.

Five current squad members, for example, played in the 5-0 home defeat to Liverpool in October 2021: Bruno Fernandes, Marcus Rashford, Luke Shaw, Harry Maguire and Diogo Dalot.

That defeat was seen as a historic nadir, which played a significant part in Ole Gunnar Solskjaer being dispensed with.

Such an embarrassment has instead become relatively routine. United have suffered another three thrashings to their biggest rivals since: 4-0, 7-0 and, on Sunday, 4-0.

That is a lot to carry. You almost could see it in the latest, the weight of all of this just bearing down as yet another huge match was spiralling towards humiliation. The facial expressions said enough.

One insider is adamant that they don’t just need a clear-out, but to actually go and sign 10 players in one window.

The club are at least thinking about January, although that hasn’t necessarily filled industry figures with much confidence. Certain inquiries have instead raised eyebrows, as United seem to be going for some players they don’t appear to greatly need.

A further potential issue is the strategy.

Various sources say the club splits targets into two main categories: “value” signings, who can deepen the squad and grow, and “superstars”.

That again makes a certain logic in the right context, but not this one. One internal view is that the starting bracket of the superstars is a mere £70m.

That’s what Liverpool were paying for Virgil van Dijk almost a decade ago.

Now, in the words of one source, it just about gets you a Nick Woltemade or a Viktor Gyokeres.

And then, many of those moves take you deeper and deeper into this same cycle: spend worse, get worse, need to spend again, on a more restricted budget.

There’s this time the danger this long-term cycle spins out of control, and maybe into relegation.

It’s why Pochettino, for now, looks like he has to forget his ideals. He just has to get a hold on this, and lock everything down.

And yet that’s just one of many big decisions this club still has to take.

The former Ajax, Fulham, Juventus and Manchester United goalkeeper suffered a brain haemorrhage in 2023

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Edwin van der Sar has his wife to thank for quickly spotting the symptoms when he suffered a brain haemorrhage in 2023.

The former Ajax, Juventus, Fulham and Manchester United great has since gone on to make a full recovery, and appeared for an Ajax Legends side against their Barcelona counterparts at the Johan Cruyff Arena last weekend.

But at the time it happened, Van der Sar's wife, Annemarie van Kesteren, knew exactly what was happening having suffered a brain haemorrhage herself back in 2009.

Van der Sar told FourFourTwo: "Annemarie knew what was happening. I had this strange feeling that something wasn't right.

"Then before you know it, you see the light and the light hurts your eyes. I had pain in my head.

"From that point onwards, you just let yourself go, and hope the ambulance and the people around you take care of you.

"You have to put your faith, your life, into the hands of people who are trained for that and who specialise in it."

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

In a way, Van der Sar considers the timing to be fortuitous: he had only recent resigned as Ajax chief executive after seven years in the post.

He said: "I'd stepped away five or six weeks before [from Ajax], so I had all the time in the world to recover, rest and get better.

"If I'd still had the job, I think the eagerness and the demands of the position might have made my recovery harder.

"When you're responsible for a club, a company or an organisation, you want to be there.

"Luckily, I had no ties and nothing else to focus on apart from myself and my recovery. I've had a few chats - but nothing has really felt right.

"I'm enjoying my life at the moment, and I'm not actively looking for another position."

Steven Chicken has been working as a football writer since 2009, taking in stints with Football365 and the Huddersfield Examiner. Steven still covers Huddersfield Town home and away for his own publication, WeAreTerriers.com. Chema Andres is quickly making Brighton fans forget about Carlos Baleba

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If there’s one thing Brighton and Hove Albion know how to do, it’s sell players for sizeable fees and replace them with bargain signings who prove to be just as good, if not better.

They replaced Yves Bissouma with Moises Caicedo, Robert Sanchez with Bart Verbruggen, Leandro Trossard with Kaoru Mitoma, and Marc Cucurella with Pervis Estupinan. Even when Caicedo and Alexis Mac Allister departed in the same summer, Brighton managed to maintain their upward trajectory thanks in part to the emergence of Carlos Baleba.

Now, having sold Baleba to Manchester United for £70 million, the Seagulls appear to have pulled off the same trick with another promising young midfielder: Chema Andres, who has developed a formidable partnership with veteran Pascal Gross in midfield.

Andres was still developing in Real Madrid’s academy less than two years ago. After honing his skills in the Spanish capital, he joined Stuttgart in 2025 for €3 million, where he quickly established himself as an important figure in midfield, steering them to a DFB-Pokal final and Champions League qualification.

He appeared destined to continue his development in Germany, but Brighton had other ideas. With just hours left in the summer transfer window, the Seagulls swooped in and signed him for £16 million. Fabian Hurzeler thrust him in at the deep end, and Andres quickly repaid his trust by assisting on his debut at Coventry and leading Brighton to an EFL Cup victory at Old Trafford.

A midfield masterclass from @BHAFC's Chema Andres 👏 https://t.co/9s4FUF7Kd2October 3, 2026

In just his second season of senior football, Andres is emerging as one of the Premier League’s top midfielders. Brighton sit second in the table, five points behind Arsenal, one ahead of Manchester City and 14 clear of relegation-threatened Manchester United. At the heart of their start is Andres, whose defensive discipline and penetrative passing has made him indispensable after Baleba's departure.

While Baleba’s greatest strength lies in his ball-carrying ability, Andres offers Brighton a different route through opposition defenses. According to Gradient Sports, a football analysis company, Andres is averaging 4.41 midfield line-breaking passes per 90 minutes, compared with Baleba’s 2.74 during his final season at Brighton. He is also completing 79.2% of these passes, well above Baleba’s 70.9%.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

That superiority extends to more audacious, high-risk passes: Andres is attempting 2.02 attacking line-breaking passes per 90, nearly twice Baleba’s 1.05, while completing them with far greater accuracy (90.9% vs. 71.4%). Whereas Baleba relied on his explosive acceleration to bypass opponents, Andres is using his vision, composure and passing range to slice through defensive lines and find his teammates.

Andres is also making his presence felt off the ball. While he might not be the same all-action midfielder who thrives on charging around the pitch and throwing himself into duels, his positional awareness and anticipation have proved invaluable in shielding Brighton’s backline. No Premier League midfielder has registered more tackles per 90 (3.31) or blocks per 90 (2.94) than Andres this season, while his 64.7% success rate in 50/50 duels exceeds Baleba’s 62.5%.

At 21 years-old, Andres is already imposing himself against the Premier League’s top sides. He excelled against Bruno Guimaraes and Declan Rice and found the back of the net in a 3–0 victory against defending champions Arsenal, before holding his own in a 1-0 win against Manchester City.

Despite costing Brighton less than a tenth of what City spent on Ayyoub Bouaddi, Elliot Anderson and Enzo Fernandez combined, Andrés helped the Seagulls secure their first away victory against City in 18 attempts, before playing a pivotal role in their hard-fought 2–0 win against Brentford.

For all his virtues, it would be premature to declare Andrés an outright upgrade on Baleba. Nevertheless, his passing intelligence, defensive anticipation and tactical discipline could make him an even better fit for Hurzeler’s system. Rather than simply replacing Baleba’s qualities, Brighton have found a midfielder whose strengths complement their style of play, once again demonstrating their knack for staying one step ahead of the transfer market.

For a club that has built its reputation on unearthing hidden gems, molding them into stars, and selling them for astronomical profits, Andres is shaping up to be another transfer masterstroke. And if he can help Brighton secure a maiden Champions League qualification, Baleba’s departure might be remembered not as a setback, but as the catalyst for the greatest moment in the club’s history.

After getting his big breakthrough as the co-founder of the football analytics website Breaking The Lines, Zachary Lowy has been able to tap into his footballing expertise for a number of esteemed outlets like ESPN, FotMob, The Times, The Independent and Urban Pitch. Since joining FourFourTwo as a freelancer in 2025, Lowy has been able to cover a wide range of topics from analyzing the sweeping changes to the MLS season to interviewing key figures like Asamoah Gyan and Rob Holding. Fluent in Spanish, Portuguese and Italian, Lowy’s versatile skillset has allowed him to traverse a number of different fields when covering major competitions like the FIFA Club World Cup. In addition to football, he is also a seasoned participant of other sports like pickleball, tennis, and volleyball.

#913. Iran war oil shock drives dip in global emissions, study shows

Global carbon emissions are expected to fall slightly in 2026, but not because of major progress on climate action. Instead, it's high energy prices following the US attack on Iran that's driving the trend.

Global carbon emissions are set to slightly drop this year, a new study suggests, largely as a result of high energy prices in the wake of the US war on Iran and the disruption of supply through the Strait of Hormuz.

Emissions from oil, gas and coal are the main drivers of climate change. While over the past decade, these emissions have risen by 0.9% per year, they are expected to drop by 0.4% in 2026.

"It's downwards, which sounds good, but this is largely driven by the war in Iran, what's happened in the Strait of Hormuz," said the study's co-author Glen Peters, a scientist at the CICERO Center for International Climate Research in Norway.

"So in a way, a little bit of good news, but for the wrong reasons."

The study was released while global leaders are meeting in Turkey for the United Nations' COP31 climate conference.

The study published by international research group the Global Carbon Project found that oil emissions dropped by 1.9% in 2026, while natural gas fell by 0.3%. Coal emissions however continued to rise, by around 0.6%.

"A drop in emissions in ‌one year is not a peak unless it ‌is driven ​by structural change," Peters cautioned.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

A structural change would mean that emissions would slowly rise to a peak and then slowly decline afterward, indicating a long term trend. That's not what happened though, Peters said. "What we see this year is [that] oil emissions are going up and then suddenly, bang, down 2%."

It is the third time in recent years that global carbon pollution has dropped. The previous declines were during the global economic crisis in 2009 and during the COVID pandemic in 2020. In each of those cases, emissions went back up once global economies recovered.

While the geopolitical shocks of the past year have been the driving factors behind the temporary emissions reversal, there has also been a rise in renewable energy contributing to the data. So while solar panels, wind farms and electric vehicles did make a difference, they were just not enough to cut emissions by themselves.

"The long-term answer remains the rapid deployment of clean energy technologies," according to co-author of the study, Pierre Friedlingstein, of the Global Carbon Budget Office at the University.

And even though emissions from fossil fuels dropped slightly, overall global carbon dioxide emissions still went up by about 1%, the study warns. The overall rise is because of land use changes like deforestation and peat fires, which increased too fast to be offset by the slight decrease in fossil fuel burning.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Jeff Stelling hosted Soccer Saturday for 29 years between 1994 and 2023 – but the end of his tenure has given him the opportunity to explore the world this year.

Stelling is currently starring in BBC One show Celebrity Race Across The World, having recently travelled from Borneo to Malaysia alongside his son Matt.

The rules of the expedition, however, meant Stelling wasn’t allowed to contact home or find out the scores of his beloved Hartlepool United.

Among the competition in the other three pairs were singers Sam Ryder and Ella Eyre, plus the offspring of Katie Price and Peter Andre, although Stelling admits to FourFourTwo that the show wasn’t exactly relaxed.

“It was incredibly stressful, because you’ve got no phone, you can’t find the football scores – no credit cards, £26 a day between the two of you for transport, food and accommodation, and you find yourself sleeping on floors, surrounded by rats in some cases,” he told us.

“But you see the most incredible sights, things I didn’t know existed. It was an amazing experience.”

Even in the remote north of Australia, Stelling still heard the familiar catchphrase of 'Unbelievable, Jeff!' – once coined by his Soccer Saturday pal Chris Kamara.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

“Wherever I go, someone will shout it and laugh as if it’s the first time it’s ever been done…” Stelling smiles – in this week’s episode, it was clear that hearing the catchphrase cheered him up, after a tough few days of travelling.

“It became part of football terminology – could you believe from the beginnings of Soccer Saturday that, 30 years later, people still use it? When I was in Australia, a gang of guys outside a hostel shouted it.”

Stelling travelled with his son on this occasion, having previously ventured to far-flung places with Kamara – heading to Sri Lanka on World’s Most Dangerous Roads.

If he’d had to choose a former footballer to travel with for Celebrity Race Across The World, who would have been the worst person he could have chosen?

“Oh, Gabby Agbonlahor,” Stelling replies instantly with a laugh, referencing his talkSPORT colleague. “His geographical knowledge isn’t quite of the standard required. He couldn’t do Race Across Birmingham!”

Stelling was speaking to FFT at the home of Woking FC as part of National League’s title sponsor Enterprise’s Local Legends campaign.

Nominations are being invited for unsung heroes across the league’s three divisions, with six eventually chosen to have their faces displayed on Wembley Way on National League play-off final weekend in May. Enterprise will also donate to community or charitable initiatives of all six associated clubs.

“In the National League, and National League North and South, virtually every club is the heartbeat of the community – there’s no other occasion when so many people from different walks of life within that community will be together,” says Stelling, whose boyhood club returned to the National League in 2023.

“Watching Hartlepool isn’t always therapeutic, but there’s nothing bigger in the community than Hartlepool United.

“For clubs like us, when the good times are so few and far between, you remember them far better. When we won promotion from the National League to the Football League in 2021, it was one of the greatest days of my life.”

There will be more from Stelling on his career in football in the next issue of FourFourTwo magazine.

#911. Fifa awards 2031 Women’s World Cup to USA-led four-country bid

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The USA, Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica will co-host the 2031 finals

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

The US-led bid to host the Women’s World Cup in 2031 was rubber-stamped at an Extraordinary Fifa Congress on Monday, while the UK will host the 2035 edition.

Both were the sole bids for those years, with their host status formally approved by a largely symbolic vote by acclamation.

The US will be one of four nations co-hosting in 2031, alongside Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica, while England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland will co-host four years later, the format following along the lines of this summer’s widely-spread men’s tournament in the US, Mexico and Canada.

In keeping with the huge expansion of football in recent years both tournaments will feature 48 teams and 104 matches, on par with this summer’s men’s World Cup. The Women’s World Cup expanded to 32 teams for the 2023 edition, which will remain the case for Brazil 2027, meaning the Women’s World Cup will double in size over a period of 16 years.

“This will be the largest women’s sporting event in history,” the US Soccer Federation president, Cindy Parlow Cone, told Fifa members in a pre-vote presentation at the governing body's headquarters in Zurich. “Which means we have to deliver.”

The US-led 2031 project across the Concacaf regional soccer body provided a choice of stadia in 20 cities: 14 in the US, four in Mexico plus San Jose in Costa Rica and Kingston, Jamaica.

The US previously hosted the Women's World Cup alone in 1999 and 2003. The national team's tournament win in 1999 was the second of its four titles.

For the second time in less than two years, Fifa has confirmed a double award of World Cup hosts without rival bids. In December 2024 member federations were asked to rubber-stamp the unprecedented six-nation, three-continent bid for the men’s World Cup in 2030 from Spain, Portugal, Morocco, Argentina, Paraguay and Uruguay.

That cleared the way for Fifa to award also the 2034 World Cup to Saudi Arabia in a fast-track process that seemed designed to exclude other candidates.

#910. ‘I had felt overconfident’: senior scientists reveal mistakes that aided discovery

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Meghie Rodrigues is a science and climate journalist in Paraná, Brazil.

Physicist Peter Shawhan and his team perfected not finding gravitational waves at the Laser Interferometer Gravitational Wave Observatory (LIGO) facility in Livingston, Louisiana — until they did. Credit: Igor Andreoni/Peter Shawhan

To err is human, science endeavours included. Accounts of missteps in the laboratory or field abound among early-career researchers, as do tales of what they learnt from them. But senior scientists make mistakes, too — and not just early in their careers.

Sometimes, reaching a dead end was the only way around a problem. Other times, graduate students saved their advisers from throwing away ‘wrong’ data. Senior scientists also know the dangers of overthinking and how it can lead to experimental paralysis. “Every year, I devote a meeting with students and postdocs to discuss failures and how errors of judgement or methods are part of academic life,” says Catherine Badgley, a palaeontologist at the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor. “I hope this helps them to see they can learn from mistakes rather than be devastated by them.”

Nature’s careers team spoke to Badgley and four other senior scientists to hear about their ‘failures’ and the lessons they took from them.

Physicist at the University of Maryland in College Park and a deputy spokesperson for the Laser Interferometer Gravitational Wave Observatory (LIGO) scientific collaboration.

For the past 26 years, I have been searching for gravitational waves with LIGO, which has a gravitational-wave observatory in Livingston, Louisiana. These waves are echoes of massive events such as the merging of black holes or the collision of neutron stars. They produce ripples in space-time and, by the time these tiny ripples reach Earth, they are so faint that scientists need extra help to ‘hear’ them, because they are extremely hard to detect by just using light, or telescopes, to see them. For example, observations of a collision of two neutron stars with telescopes has revealed the presence of gold and platinum atoms, solving a long-standing question: what is the origin of about half of all elements heavier than iron? The detection of such an event with LIGO would get us even more information.

In the first tests of LIGO, the team found nothing. Later, with improved detectors, we still found nothing.

In fact, we got very good at reporting nothing. We became experienced with knowing what we could rule out. By the time we made our first wave detection, in 2015, a finding that earned LIGO founders a physics Nobel in 2017, we had published about 100 papers reporting null results.

One such null case was in 2010. We were completing a science run, in which data are collected for a set period of time, and had a candidate for a striking event — it looked like we’d finally got there. But we knew it might be a ‘blind injection’, which is when a false signal is inserted into a data set by authorized colleagues to test our analyses.

We finished the analysis, drafted the paper and then asked the LIGO director to open a sealed envelope to tell us whether this was a real event or not. It wasn’t, but the exercise showed a real problem: the sky location our analysis recovered didn’t match the signal’s known location. Two of the detector’s mirrors had moved in the wrong direction. We found the glitch in about a day. This showed we could efficiently self-correct when detecting a real sign — which happened five years later.

I tell my students that scientists make lots of mistakes. We’re careful with cross-checks and analyse results carefully, so we catch almost all of them. Some are caught in minutes, some in days and some take more work. This one, because we’d built a test designed to assess itself, took about a day. That’s really the goal: not avoiding mistakes, but rather building enough ways to catch them quickly. Knowing what it means to find nothing is important; it’s a real scientific skill.

Chemist Omar Yaghi (second row, fifth from right), with his team at Tsinghua University in Beijing, says that professors can learn important lessons from their students if they listen to them.Credit: Yaghi Group Photo

Chemist at Tsinghua University in Beijing and a co-recipient of the 2025 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for his work with metal–organic frameworks.

Back in the 1990s, I was an assistant professor at Arizona State University in Tempe. My team had begun research trying to make inorganic porous materials. These are solid materials with a network of tiny, connected pores that act like molecular sponges to trap molecules, such as wastewater contaminants and toxic gases, on their surfaces. We were successful: we had a paper1 published in the Journal of the American Chemical Society and, later, in Science2.

Then a doctoral student came looking to join my lab. She didn’t sound very confident, her English was not so good and it wasn’t the right time of year to look for a PhD adviser. I made up some reason not to take her. But she kept coming back and was adamant about working with me.

So I accepted her into my lab group, and she started working on metal–organic compounds, another type of porous material. I felt that this was a waste of time: researchers had known about these structures since the 1950s, but nothing useful had resulted from them. Once you emptied their solvent-filled pores to trap other molecules, such as gases, they collapsed and became useless. I used to call them sculptures: they had beauty, but no function.

She kept at it, and I held onto my scepticism. After a year, we sat down to discuss her results. That was when I realized that there was an opportunity there: we could make robust metal–organic compounds, after all.

Metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) are also materials full of tiny pores. But what makes them particularly interesting is that scientists can adjust the size and shape of those pores, as well as the chemical properties inside them. This makes MOFs more tunable than inorganic porous materials such as zeolites and much better at trapping some gases. Some MOFs can drive chemical reactions, some conduct electricity and some are stable enough to be reused.

My student found strong chemical bindings that gave stability to early versions of these structures and, within a very short period, our findings were published in Nature3. It had worked.

Decades later, I met with my former student, and she told me that she had been struggling back then and wanted to try her luck with me, a new professor at the time, because no one else would take her in.

I think science is the greatest equalizer. One discovery can take you from humble beginnings, as it did for us, and propel you to the top of your profession.

I had an opinion about an area of research and didn’t listen to my student, and, to that student’s credit, she persisted. To my credit, I changed my thinking. Neither the student nor the professor can afford to do science without the other.

Plant geneticist Chris Martine’s misidentified sample led to the identification of a new species of bush tomato plant in northern Australia. Credit: Jason Cantley

Plant geneticist at Bucknell University in Lewisburg, Pennsylvania, and president of the Botanical Society of America.

I’ve studied Australia’s bush tomatoes for about 25 years. My team was the first to describe Solanum ossicruentum, nicknamed the blood bone tomato because it seems to bleed when cut open. It got us some press coverage and was a big deal for our laboratory in 20164.

In 2017, Angela McDonnell, a postdoc, joined us. We started a big genetics project to build an evolutionary tree to understand the family history of the bush tomatoes we had been studying for years. We had two samples of S. ossicruentum from two locations: the Tanami Desert and the Keep River National Park, both in northern Australia. When the results of testing came back, genomic differences landed them in totally different places on the evolutionary tree of the group.

In my mind, there was no way it was possible. I’d identified the specimens myself. I assumed we’d mislabelled something. I asked Angela to check everything carefully, but she was certain that wasn’t the case. To me it didn’t add up — I came close to saying, “let’s just pull the misplaced one and call it an error”.

Two years ago, while looking through the folders of S. ossicruentum specimens at the Northern Territory Herbarium in Palmerston, Australia, I noticed some that had strange dots on the backs of their leaves. At first, I thought it was mildew, but then I wondered whether these dots were extrafloral nectaries, or nectar-producing glands found outside the plant’s flower. Then I realized the plants with such dots were mostly from one part of Australia, the northern edge of the Tanami Desert — exactly where I was heading next.

When I got there, plants with these little dots were dripping with nectar with ants harvesting it, an interaction I hadn’t seen to this level before. I checked whether Angela’s big phylogeny project had anything from that region, and there it was — the misplaced plant. The two samples of what I thought were S. ossicruentum belonged in two different places on the evolutionary tree because they were two different species. Indeed, that initial sample’s evolutionary tree placement was the best evidence for the new species that we later described: Solanum nectarifolium5. My first thought was to thank Angela for not pulling that specimen out of our analysis. I was honestly thrilled.

Before that, I had felt overconfident in what I knew, and Angela was certain that this was a carefully curated data set and a rigorously achieved genetic result. As I’ve become more senior, I’ve become more comfortable with uncertainty: when something doesn’t fit our preconceived ideas, that’s an interesting result — that’s how you find more new things.

Now I realize how important it is for people who are more junior than myself to speak up and share their ideas, especially when they run counter to convention. If we look back at the history of science, that’s the only way we’ve progressed.

Palaeontologist Catherine Badgley says that a key skill for scientists is knowing when to stop pursuing a good idea that simply isn’t working. Credit: David Bay

Palaeontologist at the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor.

In the 1990s, I was an associate research scientist in the University of Michigan’s Museum of Paleontology. Serge Legendre, a colleague who was then at the University of Montpellier in France, showed me a new way, at the time, of explaining body-size distributions in fossils of extinct mammalian species. He used cenograms — a graphical technique that ranks mammalian species in a community by body size.

In well-watered ecosystems, there was a fairly continuous line: all species were closely spaced in size. But habitats with long dry seasons had a big gap in the middle where medium-sized mammals would be — an interesting mystery. Legendre found that many animals in that size range are fruit-eaters, and fruit isn’t available in arid or very cold environments all year long. If the theory was correct, we might be able to infer past climate from the sizes of mammals in fossil communities.

I had a lot of climate data for mammal locations worldwide, so the two of us, as well as palaeontologist Philip Gingerich, who was then also at the University of Michigan, decided to build a much larger database of locations and add climate variables. We wanted to determine whether climate variables could predict the size gap we saw. I was excited enough that I wrote it up as a book proposal and received a contract from the University of Chicago Press.

But the more data that we collected, the fuzzier the picture became. After more than a year, I had written four chapters. But I had to admit we had fewer results than when we started.

I knew the data weren’t flawed because I had used this enormous mammalian fossil database successfully for other research projects. For example, undergraduate students used it to show that the length of the growing season, as a climate variable, could be used to predict the number of fruit- and plant-eating species at a given time.

I eventually realized that each continent has its own evolutionary history and its own climatic circumstances — no one is exactly like another. Our largest data sets, from Africa and North America, have almost completely non-overlapping climates, so one was never going to be a good model for predicting the other.

Arsenal are moving for a potential superstar, as they welcome a wonderkid to North London

Arsenal are causing a “transfer frenzy” in South America, over a highly-rated wonderkid.

That's according to a new report that says that the Premier League champions are looking to improve their squad over the long term, as much as they are interested in adding players who can help the team fight on three fronts.

FourFourTwo understands that manager Mikel Arteta is keen to add dynamic difference makers in attack – but Arsenal could well surprise everyone by adding a 19-year-old who isn't well-known to Premier League fans.

During Arteta's early tenure as manager, the Gunners leant into the South American market, bringing in Pablo Mari from Flamengo as the Basque boss's first signing, six months after landing Gabriel Martinelli from the fourth tier of Brazilian football.

Since then, Arteta has built around the likes of Gabriel Jesus and Gabriel Magalhaes, while bringing in Argentine assistant Gabriel Heinze.

The champions may be about to land their first Paraguayan, too, with Sport Witness relaying reports that teenage sensation Eduardo Delmas could be on his way to London.

Delmas's club, Olimpia, meanwhile, are looking for a record sale for their talent, with the likes of Real Madrid and Paris Saint-Germain also scouting the talent.

Arteta may well be able to offer a pathway to the first team that the other two can't, however, with the likes of Max Dowman and Marli Salmon both making regular senior appearances for the Gunners after emerging recently from the famed Hale End academy.

During Arteta's time in charge, the likes of Bukayo Saka, Emile Smith Rowe and Eddie Nketiah have all played prominent roles, while Ethan Nwaneri, Folarin Balogun and Myles Lewis-Skelly have all been given Premier League debuts before the age of 21, to demonstrate Arsenal's commitment to developing youngsters.

The report suggests that “Olimpia will include numerous performance bonuses so that the operation could be worth even more than his current release clause,” though the initial fee will be a significant one, too.

#908. Why malnutrition can go unnoticed, and what that means for our health

More than 2 billion people worldwide suffer from nutrient deficiencies, most of them in the Global South. The health consequences can be devastating.

Some 50,000 deaths can be attributed to malnutrition in Germany each year, according to the German Society for Nutritional Medicine (DGEM).

The problem is that malnutrition often doesn't become apparent until the consequences are already severe.

"In most cases, you don't notice anything at first," said Matthias Pirlich, a nutritional expert and internal medicine specialist, who once served as DGEM vice president. "You could have a severe vitamin D deficiency for months before any symptoms appear at all. The same applies for vitamin B12. By the time symptoms appear, such as nerve damage, it's already too late."

A long-term B12 deficiency can damage the spinal cord, leading to numbness in the limbs, muscle weakness or even paralysis. Less common deficiency-related brain damage can cause memory loss and mental health issues.

All B vitamins play an important role in metabolism, blood formation and healthy nerve function.

Vitamins, along with various minerals such as calcium, magnesium, iron, iodine and zinc, are classed as micronutrients. The body needs to source them from food, as it cannot produce them itself. Our bodies also need macronutrients like carbohydrates, carbohydrates, protein and fats that provide us with energy.

If the body consumes less food than it needs to maintain all bodily functions over a prolonged period of time, then this is known as undernutrition. A recent World Food Organization (FAO) report estimates that approximately 645 million people worldwide suffer from chronic undernutrition.

Malnutrition, on the other hand, occurs when we consume enough calories but lack certain macronutrients or micronutrients in our food. This, too, can make one sick over time and even prove fatal. About 2 billion people worldwide suffer from this so-called hidden hunger, most of them in the Global South. That said, even some people in industrialized nations lack important micronutrients in their nutrition.

One study, for instance, found that just under three-quarters of the US population did not meet the recommended daily intake of vitamin D between 2007 and 2010, with more than two-thirds falling short of the recommended amount of vitamin E. And in Germany, about one-third of the population suffered from vitamin D deficiency in 2017, according to the German Nutrition Society. Such deficiency can cause bone, joint and muscle pain. It may also lead to an increased risk of falls and bone fractures.

About one-third of Germans also had an insufficient intake of iodine, a trace element that is indispensable for the production of thyroid hormones. Iodine deficiency can therefore disrupt normal thyroid function. Not only that — during pregnancy, a baby's brain and nervous system can only properly develop with an adequate supply of iodine.

The cultivation of agricultural produce with partially long shelf life or high yields has in some cases caused a decrease in the micronutrient content of fruits, vegetables and grains. Whether this drop in micronutrients is impacting human health, however, is a matter of debate.

Malnutrition can result from an unbalanced diet that, while filling and providing energy, lacks essential micronutrients. Examples of such empty calories include fast food and highly processed foods, as well as white bread and white rice.

Poverty is often the reason for such an unbalanced diet, for example when people in the Global South can only afford to buy staples such as flour or rice.

Another study found that in Germany, households at risk of poverty are more likely to consume foods that are low in nutrients and high in calories.

Depression is also associated with an increased risk of nutrient deficiency. "People often lose their appetite, and when they neglect their self-care, they may end up eating a very unbalanced diet," Pirlich told DW. His research shows that older adults and people who live alone often develop malnutrition, too. The risk also increases the more medications a person takes.

Many diseases result in the body being less efficient at absorbing or utilizing nutrients through the intestines. This applies to people with inflammatory or chronic disease, such as Crohn's disease, celiac disease, liver disease and cancer.

The DGEM estimates that some 30% of all patients receiving inpatient care in Germany are affected by or at risk of malnutrition. Yet health insurance data shows that only about 1% of patients are screened and treated for nutrient deficiencies.

Often, patients' malnutrition worsens during their hospital stay. The consequences can be serious, potentially causing additional complications, delayed recuperation, longer hospital stays and even increased mortality rates. This results in higher healthcare expenditure, amounting to billions each year.

German policymakers and medical associations are therefore developing a plan to better screen for and treat malnutrition in hospitals. The road map will be ready by 2027 and copy the Dutch approach in the sense that all patients are checked for nutritional deficiencies upon hospital admission.

Pirlich wants to see such screenings for at-risk groups in outpatient clinics, too: "This includes all those with chronic and serious illnesses and, above all, older adults."

To prevent poverty-related malnutrition, Pirlich suggests increased access to healthy food, offering free school meals as an example.

The nutritional expert recommends eating a diet that is varied and largely plant-based. "Secondary plant compounds have a very positive effect, and if you eat a highly diverse diet, you consume many different foods that are [nutritionally] beneficial," said Pirlich.

There's a simple rule of thumb: The more colorful your food, the better.

Also, cook vegetables as gently as possible, because overheating and keeping them warm for too long destroys their vitamins. Long storage periods also lead to vitamin loss, so it makes sense to go for seasonal and regional foods in particular.

But even when ensuring a healthy and balanced diet, some people still develop a nutrient deficiency. A blood test can provide clarity, and dietary supplements may help make up for the deficiency.

This article was originally written in German.

#907. Gianni Infantino’s controversial World Cup sell-off plan was ‘set to run for 96 years’

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Infantino scrapped his plan in August following significant backlash

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

A controversial plan proposed by Gianni Infantino to establish Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) would have transferred commercial rights for the World Cup for up to 96 years, according to leaked documents.

First revealed in a report by The Times on 28 July, the project – which involved private investors taking a minority stake – was dropped by Infantino on 1 August following opposition from three continental confederations.

Fifa had previously confirmed in July that the private investment group was to be led by Thrive Capital, a firm established by Joshua Kushner, the brother of United States President Donald Trump’s son-in-law.

Reports published on Monday by The Guardian and the New York Post cited leaked files showing that all commercial rights for Fifa competitions would have been handed to FFE for commercial exploitation over a 96-year period.

The Guardian reported that the contract was structured on a rolling basis up to a maximum of 96 years, with the New York Post adding that only a severe contract breach by FFE could terminate the agreement.

Both outlets reported details of an FFE management bonus pool, which could have awarded $50 million (£38.3m) for every $1 billion added to the initial $20bn valuation of the business.

The files also indicated that the board of FFE was to be chaired by the sitting Fifa president, a position currently held by Infantino.

A Fifa spokesperson said: "Fifa has consistently stated that the Fifa Forward Enterprise proposal would have been subject to the approval of the Fifa Member Associations and the Fifa Council.

"For the avoidance of doubt, any potential Management Incentive Plan was exclusively for members of FFE management, of which Fifa officials could not have been part. This is customary for proposed structures of this nature.

"Fifa’s leadership would only have had leading roles in the board, which would not have led to any additional remuneration. The remuneration of the Fifa President is set by the independent compensation sub-committee.

"Fifa intends to reply to questions submitted by its Council members and has no intention of breaching confidentiality by commenting first to media."

Fifa has invited Council members to review files relating to FFE at its Zurich headquarters.

Football Association chair and Fifa vice-president Debbie Hewitt intends to accept, though she and other European representatives on the Council are seeking clarity regarding which documents will be available, the review protocols, and non-disclosure terms.

Meanwhile, Uefa has lodged applications in the US legal system seeking document disclosure from Fifa, Thrive, and advising bank JP Morgan, with a view to possible Swiss criminal proceedings.

Fifa has described Uefa’s court filings as a "smear campaign".

Uefa stated in August that it had "lost confidence" in Infantino over the FFE proposal and has backed French Football Federation president Philippe Diallo to challenge the Swiss official in next year’s election.

However, Infantino remains the firm favourite to win a fourth term at the Fifa Congress in Rabat, Morocco next March.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Harry Kane is England’s new leading appearance-maker after passing Peter Shilton’s record last week – and he hasn’t been the only player tipped to reach the milestone over the years.

Shilton’s record of 125 Three Lions caps had stood since he made his final appearance for his country at the 1990 World Cup, before Kane played his 126th cap against Croatia, then made it 127 against Spain on Sunday.

Wayne Rooney had previously finished agonisingly short on 120, with David Beckham winning 115 caps, Steven Gerrard reaching 114, Ashley Cole making it to 107 and Frank Lampard clocking up 106.

Another player who looked on course to surpass Shilton at one point was Michael Owen, who won his 89th cap at the age of just 28, but didn’t add to his tally as injuries derailed his career.

Asked whether he feels he would have made it to 126 if the injuries hadn’t hit, the former striker is philosophical about it.

“I’m not that bothered about that, I had my time,” he told FFT. “In little moments when you think back over your career, you think of things, but that’s across the board, isn’t it?

“If I didn’t get injured then, would I have won more Golden Boots? Would I have won the Ballon d’Or more? Would I have won more of anything? You just never know. It’s one of those things.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

“There’s no question about it, if I had Harry Kane’s constitution, there’s no doubt I would have scored many, many, many more goals than I did, played many, many, many more games than I did, and all the rest of it.

“But I’m happy with my lot, I played 89 times for England – that’s quite a lot. That’s just life, isn’t it? You can’t spend your life thinking ‘What if?’”

Owen reserved praise for Kane, who has scored an incredible 93 goals during his 127 caps.

“What he’s done is extraordinary really,” Owen said, speaking in association with soccer betting odds. “He’s fine-tuned his game to become one of the most lethal players on the planet. It’s strange because he’s not the fastest, he’s not got a trick that always beats a defender, it’s pure efficiency.

“His finishing is just lethal. I think he’s the best finisher on the planet by some way, whether it’s left foot, heading, placing the ball, power, his penalties are brilliant. He’s practised and practised all his life to become so elite.

“You need so many things when you’re a player. A lot of it comes naturally, but you need to hone your skills as well. Harry has been one of the most hard-working players of this generation and deserves everything he gets.”

#903. LaLiga hit by cyber attack with fans’ personal data exposed

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The breach occurred between 14 and 16 November

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

A cyber attack has compromised personal data stored on a LaLiga digital platform, Spain's top football league confirmed in an official statement on Monday.

The precise scale of the breach, which occurred between 14 and 16 November, remains unknown. However, LaLiga stated that personal data from both a fan platform and individual football clubs were affected during the incident.

The matter has been escalated to the Spanish Agency for the Protection of Data, as well as reported to the National Police's Central Unit of Cyber-Delinquency.

LaLiga discovered the cyber incident on 16 November and immediately implemented measures to contain it.

The organisation's IT security personnel are currently evaluating platform logs to determine which specific data was compromised, while monitoring across all online systems has been stepped up to prevent further security breaches.

A number of cyber attacks have taken place across the globe in recent weeks, with the European Union (EU) confirming it had been targeted last week.

An official said cyber security specialists had been responding to an artificial intelligence-generated attack on a key EU institution for almost a month, leaving a number of the bloc's digital systems offline.

The official offered no further details on the nature of the breach or who might be responsible. It represents the first instance of the 27-member union disclosing a cyberattack carried out using an AI tool.

"AI-assisted tools can be used and especially misused to detect vulnerabilities," said Thomas Regnier, spokesperson for the European Commission, the executive branch of the 27-nation EU.

"Indeed we can confirm that this was done with AI tools," he added. "We have seen many global cyber attacks recently, and of course no one is immune to this."

Regnier noted that the EU initially detected the security incident on 22 October. Officials immediately opened an investigation while implementing "preventative measures."

The incident was first reported by news website Politico, which stated the breach lasted for at least 10 days and impacted systems used for translation, reimbursement, salaries and timesheets. Regnier declined to confirm that report.

"We temporarily took down several applications, and most of them have since then been restored," Regnier said. So far, he added, "we have not detected any evidence of a data breach affecting commission staff as a whole."
