#902. Will Australia push for fossil fuel exit at UN talks?

The heat is on Australia as chief negotiator at the COP31 UN climate conference to forge a path away from coal and gas, and to protect Pacific neighbors facing rising sea levels.

In its role as president of negotiations at the UN climate talks in Turkey, Australia is being pressured to guide nations toward unified action on slashing the greenhouse gas emissions that are generated in large part by burning fossil fuels.

The nation has pledged to lead by example at the summit through a strong commitment to renewable energy, electrification and reduced reliance on planet-heating coal, oil and gas.

"Renewable energy, grids, storage and electrification are creating opportunities to strengthen resilience, improve energy security, and reduce emissions at the same time," said Chris Bowen, Australia's climate change and energy minister, in October during a meeting in Fiji ahead of the COP climate conference.

"These are proven, commercial and scalable today. Now is the moment for faster implementation."

Yet Australia is also the world's third-largest exporter of fossil fuels. And unlike France and Germany, or island nations from Fiji to the Bahamas that are highly vulnerable to a changing climate, the COP31 co-president has not yet committed to phasing them out.

As calls grow for the country to set a clear route to a clean energy future, critics say its vague promise to transition away from polluting sources of power does not go far enough.

Australia is home to 56% of the world's coal mine projects currently in the pipeline, notes environmental nonprofit, 350.org.

Andreas Sieber, head of political strategy at the organization, is calling on the country, the world's second-largest coal exporter, to reverse course and announce an "overdue coal phaseout date" during the COP31 conference.

"Australia needs to walk the walk and follow Germany's example and commit to a phaseout," said Melanie Pill, founder of The Climate Project, an Australia-based climate policy advisory.

The argument to end fossil fuel production is not only about cutting emissions but reducing dependence on energy systems that rely on volatile oil and gas markets, she explained.

"A fossil phaseout in the face of the enduring and escalating conflict in the Middle East is in the interest of everyone," Pill told DW.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

This is especially true for Australia's diesel-reliant Pacific neighbors, who spend up to 25% of GDP on fossil fuel imports — as opposed 6% on health — according to a report by the Institute for Climate Risk and Response at the University of New South Wales.

As lead negotiator at the UN climate talks, Australia can "flip the narrative" on a fossil fuel phaseout, using the challenge of energy security as a justification, said Pill.

This opportunity could be lost, however, if Australia fails to address fossil fuel exports that accounted for 80% of its total carbon footprint in 2022 — and near 5% of global emissions.

While the nation is a world leader in rooftop solar, and generates around half of its electricity from renewables, this progress is "being undone by its continued approval of more fossil fuels for export," said Simon Bradshaw, COP31 lead and climate expert at Greenpeace Australia Pacific.

He noted that the Labor government of Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has approved the construction, expansion or extension of 38 coal, oil and gas projects since coming to power four years ago on a pro-climate platform.

"You cannot aspire to lead on climate abroad if you're not getting your own house in order," said Thomas Houlie, climate and energy policy analyst at Climate Analytics, a global climate policy institute.

In 2025, when Australia approved the extension of a major gas export project in the country's west until 2070, Albanese justified the move in the name of a balance between "security of energy supply" and "support [for] the transition which reduces our emissions."

The country has publicly backed a global transition away from the fossil fuels driving the global temperature rise linked to extreme heat and drought. Both through the Global Stocktake agreed at the 2023 UN climate summit, and via the inaugural "transitioning away" summit in Colombia this April, at which Australia and 56 countries pledged to develop a fossil fuel exit road map.

But these commitments are not reflected in Australian resources policy, or its domestic rollout of clean power infrastructure.

"While the government has set a renewables target for electricity, it leaves plenty of blind spots in other sectors," said Houlie, adding that emission reductions in industry and transport have been limited and that the push to achieve an 82% renewables target for the electricity grid by 2030 is behind schedule.

In its role as lead negotiator at COP31, Australia has promised to ensure that any final conference text serves to "elevate the views and the experiences" of small Pacific nations in its region, from Vanuatu to Tuvalu.

These island countries that generate low emissions yet suffer extreme climate impacts from worsening cyclones or rising seas are "sick of Australia's double talk on climate," said Shiva Gounden, head of Pacific at Greenpeace Australia Pacific.

Australia must commit to "substantial new funding contributions" to help Pacific neighbors adapt to the climate emergency and achieve energy independence, said his colleague Bradshaw. He reiterated the need to concurrently create a "national road map" away from coal and gas production and export.

A Climate Analytics report co-authored by Houlie outlines a fossil fuel phaseout pathway for Australia that can begin immediately. This includes an end to coal power generation by 2034 and a rapid reduction in oil and gas consumption, with renewables generating almost all the country's electricity by 2040. Fossil fuel export projects would be eliminated, and existing ones shuttered before becoming obsolete.

"This co-presidency is a golden opportunity for Australia to step up and commit to a phaseout," said Houlie.

Manchester United have notified the FA of their intention to appeal Leny Yoro's red card against Liverpool.

Mauricio Pochettino's side lost 4-0 at Anfield in the Argentine's first game in charge, and his plans went up in smoke as Yoro was dismissed inside the first eight minutes for bundling over Alexander Isak as the striker ran through on goal.

There was some debate as to whether the foul was a clear denial of the goalscoring opportunity, as it was unclear whether Isak was in control of the ball as he made his way towards the penalty area.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Under the laws of the game, one of the considerations regarding a red card for Denying of an Obvious Goalscoring Opportunity (DOGS), is the likelihood of the attacking player "keeping or gaining control of the ball".

United boss Pochettino felt that not only did Isak lose control of the ball with his touch, but also that United should have been given a penalty for Jeremy Jacquet's challenge on Bryan Mbeumo at the opposite end just moments before.

However, former Premier League referee Dermot Gallagher backed the onfield decision in both instances.

"If you look at it from the referee's angle, is it a foul? That's the first step. Yes. Is he in possession of the ball? From that angle, yes.

"I think most people would have expected a red card. It would have been a surprise during the game if a red card hadn't been given.

"I don't know if he would have got to the ball before Lammens. You watch it play out. Do you think it's a red card? Gary Neville's immediate reaction was red card."

On Mbeumo's penalty appeal: "When players are side by side, you can do that. They are side by side. Jacquet was even in front of him."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"The ball was for the goalkeeper. In that situation, if you review the VAR you can see for sure, [Yoro] never had the intention to connect with Isak.

"When the control was long with the striker, the ball was going to the goalkeeper, he runs and goes down. In Leny's case, it wasn't intentional.

"If you look before, on the sixth minute. Jacquet on Mbeumo. Similar? No. If you compare the actions, that was a penalty."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Manchester United midfielder Kobbie Mainoo on the red card:

"The game's been taken out of our hands by a red card that I don't think can be a red card," he said.

"No chance. The ball's already with the goalkeeper. They're both running full speed. What can we do? It is what it is.

"It's 10 vs 11, you come to a place like Anfield, it's a tough game anyway. Then you lose a man, it makes it hard. I can't fault the boys for their fight in the game. We take the pain and move on.

"I wouldn't say it all goes out the window. You can still take the things you did in training into the game, but it makes it 10 times harder with one less man in a situation like that."

Sky Sports' Roy Keane speaking at half-time:

"Isak's not getting the ball. There's no way he's getting the ball.

"It's clumsy from United. Obviously it's one straight ball over the top. You shouldn't be in so much trouble.

"But there's no way he's getting that ball. Absolutely not. I know Isak is quick and he's sharp, but we've looked at it again.

"It's really poor defending. Players not smelling danger. But Isak is not getting that ball. Absolutely not."

Are Liverpool prepared for Grand Theft Auto to ruin their weekend preparation?

Ah s***, here we go again: GTA VI dropped this week to rapturous acclaim from critics and public alike, with the long-awaited video game responsible for plenty of us turning up to work a little bleary-eyed after an all-nighter in Vice City.

And given that Premier League footballers are often avid gamers – they have a lot of time on their hands – FPL players are going to have to take into account those last-minute “groin strains” that see big-hitters pull out of this weekend's action…

In September 2013, Liverpool defender Daniel Agger suffered a freak abdominal injury when he overstretched to prevent a dumbbell from falling on his foot in training. Or did he?

No, he probably did: but while the story certainly made sense – and Agger even aggravated the injury after playing through the pain barrier – the fact that Grand Theft Auto V was released that week certainly led some to wonder whether the Dane had in fact pulled a sickie.

Agger was far from the only suspicious absentee that week in the league either, with high-profile names missing up and down the country.

Robin van Persie and David Silva both missed the Manchester derby, completely unexpectedly, with the stars ruled out late with sudden muscle injuries: Manchester United boss David Moyes even revealed that he'd given RVP the chance to play right up until that Sunday morning.

#899. The Women’s World Cup is coming to the UK – but what will it look like?

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The joint ‘All Together’ bid had no competition but the UK has put forward an ambitious project that would look to build on the legacy of the Lionesses

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

The United Kingdom has been confirmed as the hosts of the 2035 Women’s World Cup, in what is set to be the largest single-sport event ever to be staged in the country.

The joint “All Together” bid from the football associations of the four home nations – England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland – was approved by acclamation and officially announced during an online meeting of the Fifa Congress on Monday, although it was the only bidder in the process.

The tournament will nevertheless be the first Women’s World Cup to be staged in the UK, as well as the first football World Cup to be held in the UK since England hosted the men’s World Cup in 1966.

Although the UK will be hosting the men’s Euros in 2028, the 2035 Women’s World Cup will be twice the size in terms of competition format: with 48 teams playing 104 matches across a period of five weeks, and around 4.5 million tickets set to be available for fans.

It also promises to build on the legacy of the Lionesses, who won the Euros at Wembley in 2022 and have played in three consecutive major tournament finals – also reaching the Women’s World Cup final in 2023 and retaining the Euros in 2025.

“On behalf of the Football Associations of England, Northern Ireland, Scotland, and Wales, thank you for your trust and confidence in awarding us the Fifa Women’s World Cup 2035,” FA chair Debbie Jevans said following the confirmation.

“We’re deeply honoured by your support, and grateful for the opportunity to host the pinnacle of women’s football on behalf of the global football family. Together, we will celebrate the power of women’s football, inspire the next generation and unite fans from every corner of the world.

“We look forward to welcoming you to the United Kingdom in 2035 and to deliver an exceptional Fifa Women’s World Cup that the entire football community can be proud of.”

The Women’s World Cup only expanded to 32 teams ahead of the tournament in Australia and New Zealand in 2023; by 2031, it will expand to 48 teams – matching the format of the men’s World Cup – for the tournament in the United States, Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica. The competition will have doubled in size in the space of 16 years.

With such a strong portfolio of existing stadiums across the country, the UK’s bid “significantly exceeded” the minimum requirement of 14 venues. The original proposal includes 16 stadiums in England, three in Wales, two in Scotland and one in Northern Ireland, and some that have yet to be built.

Manchester United have signalled their ambition to host the 2035 Women’s World Cup final in their planned new 100,000-capacity stadium. But United’s timeline around the construction of the new £2bn stadium, or who is going to pay for it, remains ambiguous, so the current Old Trafford was included in the UK’s bid as well.

If the new stadium is built in time, it could mean the Women’s World Cup final is held outside London, with Wembley previously hosting the men’s World Cup final in 1966 as well as men’s and women’s Euros finals in 1996, 2021, 2022 and 2028. Prime minister Andy Burnham said he wanted Manchester to host the final when he was previously mayor of the city.

Birmingham City’s proposed Sports Quarter Stadium was also named in the UK’s bid, with plans for a 62,000-capacity stadium unveiled last year. Chelsea are exploring whether to expand Stamford Bridge or move to a new home in Earl’s Court, with their development also included in the UK’s bid.

As for existing stadiums in England, Aston Villa’s Villa Park, Brighton’s Amex Stadium, Bristol City’s Ashton Gate, Leeds United’s Elland Road, Everton’s Hill Dickinson Stadium, Manchester City’s Etihad Stadium, Newcastle’s St James’ Park, Sunderland’s Stadium of Light and Nottingham Forest’s City Ground add to an ambitious list of venues.

There are four further London venues on the list: Wembley, which could also host the final, Arsenal’s Emirates Stadium, Crystal Palace’s Selhurst Park and the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium. The Principality Stadium in Cardiff, Cardiff City’s Cardiff City Stadium and Wrexham’s Racecourse Ground are named, while Hampden Park in Glasgow, Easter Road in Edinburgh and Windsor Park in Belfast complete the proposed venues.

The final list of host cities and venues would be confirmed by Fifa closer to the start of the tournament, but the UK’s bid team said that 63 million people live within two hours of a proposed venue, making the World Cup the “most accessible tournament ever”.

By the time of the 2035 World Cup, many of the England players who played such an important role in the rise of women’s football by winning the Euros at Wembley in 2022 and becoming role models for the next generation will have likely hung up their boots.

Given that Lucy Bronze appears determined to appear at another major tournament for England next summer at the age of 35, it is not inconceivable that a 33-year-old Lauren James, or a 34-year-old Hannah Hampton, or a 35-year-old Lauren Hemp, or a 36-year-old Alessia Russo could still be representing the Lionesses by then.

But it is far more likely that the majority of the Lionesses squad for the World Cup, a tournament they have yet to win, will be built from players who are only just coming through the England pathway now and are currently representing teams from the Under-17s to the Under-23s.

Sarina Wiegman revealed she was excited about the potential of the next generation when naming her latest England squad last week. Midfielder Erica Meg Parkinson, 18, has kept her place after making her debut last month, while Chelsea’s Lexi Potter, 20, has also enjoyed a breakout year.

“Hopefully these talents go from high potential to world-class players,” Wiegman said. “While I’m talking about that, I’m getting excited. It does excite me. I hope I have a contribution to that, but it starts with the players themselves.”

After the initial wave brought through by the Lionesses, the next generation also now have a major target to aim for with a home World Cup in 2035. It could be game-changing for player development, while current stars such as Maya Le Tissier and Michelle Agyemang will look to further solidify their place in the England set-up in the years to come.

“The thought of another generation growing up knowing that the biggest stage in the game is coming to their home country is amazing,” Agyemang said. “To have the chance to play in a home World Cup would be a dream, but even more exciting is thinking about all the girls watching who might see 2035 and believe they can be part of it one day.”

One of the most pivotal figures in English football over the last decade has been Wiegman, who led the Lionesses to three consecutive major tournament finals with her run as a manager stretching to five when you include previous achievements with the Netherlands. The FA recently announced that Wiegman had extended her contract with England through to the end of Euro 2029, which will mean she had been in the job for eight years. “I tend to think that’s the end point, but you never know,” Wiegman said when asked if she could stay beyond 2029. “I don’t plan that far ahead. So let’s see where it gets to.”

Wiegman will leave enormous shoes to fill when she eventually leaves England and the task of replacing one of the best coaches in the game is a sizeable one for the FA, but there is currently no obvious succession plan. The FA should be able to produce up-and-coming English coaches as well as players, but all the top jobs in the Women’s Super League are filled by foreign managers.

However, two attractive candidates could emerge in the shape of former England international Casey Stoney, who is now in charge of Canada, while Emma Hayes, after a decade at Chelsea, is preparing to lead the United States into next summer’s World Cup. Whether they could be available in future years depends on how they perform in the next two cycles. But knowing England will be hosts of the 2035 World Cup heightens the need for the FA to plan for life after Wiegman, too.

The hope for Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland has to be that the World Cup can act as a catalyst for the growth of women’s football at home, in the same way as the Lionesses winning the Euros at Wembley in 2022 did for England.

In terms of grassroots participation and the development of domestic leagues, England’s victory four years ago was a boost for the other home nations, too, but nothing compares to the feeling of staging games in front of a nation on home soil.

The tournament could be transformative, especially when you consider that the other home nations cannot take playing in major tournaments for granted. Scotland have only appeared at a Women’s World Cup once, in 2019, while Wales made history by qualifying for their first major tournament when they reached Euro 2025 and Northern Ireland did the same when they made it through to Euro 2022.

“Wales has been a football nation for 150 years and we have never hosted anything on this scale,” said Noel Mooney, the chief executive of the Football Association of Wales. “World Cup football played here, in front of Welsh children, would change what this game looks like in Wales: in the clubs, in the schools, and in the number of girls who grow up seeing a pathway into it.”

“A Women’s World Cup in Northern Ireland would be felt in every club and every age group, in every part of the country,” the Irish Football Association’s chief executive Patrick Nelson said. “Our young players would grow up having watched the best in the world play at home, and there is no substitute for that.”

Scottish Football Association chief executive Ian Maxwell said hosting the World Cup would be “the most significant thing to happen to the women’s and girls’ game in Scotland”. He added: “The impact would go far beyond just the matches themselves. The level of investment into coaching, facilities and player pathways in the years beforehand will shape the future of the game for the generations to come.”

The announcement of the Women’s World Cup hosts was made by Fifa president Gianni Infantino, who lost the support of the English FA, Scottish FA, Welsh FA and Irish FA following his scrapped World Cup sell-off plan earlier this year. The FA chair, Debbie Hewitt, recently confirmed that they considered launching a legal challenge to Infantino’s eligibility to stand for a fourth term as Fifa president, highlighting the delicate politics that were at play while the bid for the 2035 Women’s World Cup was considered.

Infantino is standing for re-election in March and, under current rules, would be ineligible to run for a fifth term from 2031. Infantino should therefore be out of the picture by the time the UK hosts the World Cup in 2035, but they will have at least four years of working together on the World Cup if the Fifa president win his re-election bid. Infantino retains the support of the majority of Fifa’s member associations, but it’s a different story in the UK and prime minister Andy Burnham has previously called for his resignation.

There is already one area that could lead to some friction between the UK government and Fifa. The home nations’ bid received a score of 4.3 out of five in Fifa’s evaluation report. All but one of the categories – which include stadiums, transport and sustainability – were deemed “low risk” but the exception was “contractual framework”, with Fifa’s report stating “certain government guarantees contain material qualifications, particularly regarding tax and safety and security”.

The Guardian has reported that Fifa has demanded tax-free status from ticket sales and broadcast and commercial partnerships, something that the UK government has not allowed when previously hosting major events such as the 2012 Olympics and will not offer to Uefa when they stage Euro 2028. The Independent reported extensively on the huge cost many US cities faced by hosting men’s World Cup matches last summer, and the UK will be keen to ensure that it will not face similar shortfalls in nine years’ time.

The 2035 World Cup will now act as the cornerstone for transforming football for women and girls in the UK, with the government working with the football associations from the four countries on three areas: making the game more accessible to girls and under-represented communities, developing coaching, officiating and leadership, and attracting more investment into women’s football.

A joint statement from the chief executives of the four associations said: “What follows now is eight and a half years of work; on facilities, on coaching, on officiating, on the pathways that take a girl from her first game to a professional contract. The players who will light up 2035 are in our parks and playgrounds right now.”

#897. Why electrification is the climate game changer we need

From EVs and electric buses on the road, heat pumps warming homes and solar panels powering appliances, the shift to electrifying tech is already in full swing. But what exactly does "electrification" mean?

Electrification isn't just a buzzword, it's a lever that could slash energy bills while reducing the world's dependency on coal, oil and gas. Which also means significantly slashing the heat-trapping CO2 emissions that are linked to flooding and extreme heat around the world.

If fuel-importing countries "speed up the electrification of their economies considerably" they could knock more than $400 billion (€357 billion) off their energy import bills by 2035 compared with 2025 levels. That is according to a recent analysis by the International Energy Agency, which also found that such an acceleration could mean the world needs 18 million fewer barrels of oil per day.

In a nutshell, electrification means replacing technologies that burn fossil fuels such as oil and gas with electric alternatives. That means switching from diesel cars to electric vehicles (EVs), turning off gas heating and using electricity to power heat pumps.

But the way the electricity running these things is generated is also important. In theory, an EV using power created in a coal-heavy electricity grid could be worse for the climate than a car running on gas.

Electricity derived from renewable energy sources such as solar, wind or hydropower on the other hand produces clean power.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The booming EV market is the fastest-growing electrification sector. Globally, one in four cars sold in 2025 was electric and since 2020, international sales have increased by almost 600%.

Nonetheless, electricity only covers about 20% of final energy use in the wider global economy, including that used in businesses, factories and people's homes.

It would need to supply more than half of all power by 2050 if we are to avoid runaway heating and the more intense and extreme weather events connected to a hotter climate.

Some industries and activities are harder to electrify than others. While it's relatively easy to switch to EVs and decarbonize buildings, some industries such as petrochemicals and steel use fossil fuels as raw materials to make products like plastics, fertilizer, detergent or steel.

In addition, while heat pumps work well for low-temperature needs, they can't replace the temperatures needed in steelmaking or cement production.

The World Resources Institute, an independent research organization, recommends hydrogen, synthetic fuels or other low-carbon alternatives as more viable options than electrification in cases such as ocean shipping and aviation.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In addition to cutting down on greenhouse gas emissions resulting in cleaner air and limiting global heating, electrification is also more efficient and cheaper in the long run.

A combustion engine in a car wastes as much as 80% of its fuel energy, mostly to turn it into heat. Only about 20% is converted to actually move the car. Electric motors, on the other hand, convert about 80% of electrical energy into motion.

As the World Resources Institute points out, running all appliances on electricity will increase electricity consumption. Yet total energy costs are likely to be lower, even if electricity becomes more expensive.

As electricity needs grow due to the rapid expansion of AI, data centers and the overall shift to a more electrified world, outpaced grids struggle to keep up. This is increasingly holding back the energy transition, delaying the rollout of additional renewable generation, storage capacity and electrified demand.

According to the International Energy Agency, annual grid investment has to increase by about 50% by 2030 from today's $400 billion.

There's also a major mismatch between how long it takes to set up new grid infrastructure (five to 15 years), compared to renewable energy projects (one to five years), and EV charging infrastructure (one to two years).

Experts say we need smarter grids that support a two-way flow of electricity while remaining secure, stable and able to keep up with higher demand as electrification intensifies.

#896. Enzo Maresca insists Man City’s slump is ‘normal’ after Pep Guardiola exit

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Manchester City have failed to win any of their last four Premier League matches

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Enzo Maresca remains unconcerned by Manchester City’s recent slump in form, maintaining that a period of adjustment was to be expected during the club's "reset" following Pep Guardiola's departure.

After opening his debut campaign with seven consecutive Premier League wins, the manager has seen his side go four league games without a victory while trying to establish balance in midfield and defence.

The Italian coach last week rejected suggestions that City's current difficulties were connected to the club being found guilty of extensive financial breaches in a long-running legal battle with the Premier League.

Instead, he views the current issues as temporary growing pains after taking over from Guardiola.

"For me, it’s part of the process because this is like a reset," he said Monday. "It’s like a restart after 10 years with the same manager, same face, same words, same method.

"It’s not easy to suddenly, all of a sudden, change. For me personally, it’s all normal and hopefully, as soon as possible, we can find the right balance in all the lines, defense and midfield, and we can be consistent. That, for me, is the difference in this moment between us and other clubs. "

City break from domestic competition on Tuesday when they host Napoli in the Champions League.

The match brings Kevin De Bruyne back to the Etihad Stadium, with the Belgian — considered by many to be City’s greatest player — having left in the summer of 2025 after 10 years at the club.

Maresca, who coached De Bruyne while serving as assistant during City’s treble-winning campaign in 2022-23, called him "no doubt" one of the finest players he has worked with.

"Not only personally, I think also for the history of this club," Maresca said. "In the last 10 years, all the trophies the club achieved, Kevin was here and an important player, a fantastic player, a top guy, polite, fantastic. For me it was a pleasure to work to work with him."

De Bruyne previously returned to City last season in the Champions League league stage, though he was substituted after 26 minutes during Napoli's 2-0 defeat after teammate Giovanni Di Lorenzo was sent off.

Ahead of the game, Maresca confirmed that right-back Matheus Nunes is back in contention following an injury.

City sit seventh in the 36-team Champions League standings, having won three of their four league phase fixtures so far.

Washington Spirit, meanwhile, delivered the standout performance of the round, sweeping aside Portland Thorns 4-1. Trinity Rodman scored twice, while Clara Luvanga contributed a goal and two assists.

The semi-finals then saw Washington continue their impressive form with a 2-1 victory over Utah, while Kansas City knocked out defending champions Gotham with the same scorline.

Now, just one game separates the two finalists from lifting the Championship trophy, with Washington Spirit looking to make home advantage count and Kansas City Current aiming to finish their campaign on the ultimate high.

Rodman has been central to Washington's success this season, recording a career-best 12 goals and eight assists in the regular season. The forward carried that form into the quarter-finals, scoring twice and providing an assist in the 4-1 victory over Portland. She backed this up with another assist as her side overcame Utah Royals in the semi-final. Named an NWSL MVP finalist, Rodman will be one of Washington's biggest attacking threats as they look to finally get over the line after consecutive Championship final defeats.

While Temwa Chawinga will often steal the headlines, Bethune has enjoyed an outstanding season since joining Kansas City from Washington, setting a new NWSL single-season record with 11 assists. The midfielder also made a big impact in the semi-finals, scoring a stunning free-kick to open the scoring in the 2-1 victory over Gotham. Her creativity and ability to unlock opposition defences will be crucial against her former club, particularly with two-time MVP Chawinga providing a constant attacking threat alongside her.

Prediction: Washington Spirit 1-2 Kansas City Current

Washington, who were champions in 2021, will have the advantage of playing in front of their home supporters at Audi Field, but Kansas City Current have the attacking quality to spoil the occasion. Croix Bethune's creativity and Temwa Chawinga's threat in front of goal give them plenty of ways to hurt Spirit, while their semi-final victory over reigning champions Gotham will have given them a huge confidence boost.

Kansas City have unfinished business in the Championship after finishing runners-up to Portland Thorns in 2022. They have the opportunity to claim their first-ever NWSL Championship title, and with the quality throughout their squad, they could finally get their hands on the trophy. Washington will be determined to turn around their fortunes after heartbreak in back-to-back finals, but I fancy Kansas City to edge a memorable contest.

Manchester United could be set to appoint their first female coach to the men's first team.

Sílvia Tuyà travelled to Carrington alongside new manager Mauricio Pochettino, having first worked with him during his time at Chelsea and then on a permanent basis in the United States.

While she has not yet been named as part of the backroom staff, the highly-qualified sports scientist could become part of the team, although United are yet to make a final decision.

Sílvia Tuyà is a Spanish strength and conditioning coach who joined the United States men's national team setup in October 2024, shortly after Pochettino's appointment.

With a PhD in sports science from the University of Barcelona, she previously worked in women's football with FC Levante Badalona in Spain's top division, Liga F. She has also held academic positions at the University of Barcelona and the National Institute of Physical Education of Catalonia. Fluent in English, Spanish and Catalan, her qualifications include a doctorate in high performance.

Pochettino is assembling his backroom staff following his arrival at Old Trafford, bringing several trusted members of his coaching team with him from previous roles.

Tuya travelled to Carrington alongside the Argentine on Wednesday, but was notably absent from the official list of coaching appointments released by United.

The club are still considering whether to bring her into the setup, but her potential appointment would make her the first woman to coach Manchester United's men's first team.

#893. Celtic accept reduced ticket allocation for Hearts visit amid fan calls to reject offer

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Celtic have stated they will contact the SPFL over the issue

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Celtic have accepted a reduced ticket allocation for their upcoming visit to Tynecastle amid calls from fans to reject the offer.

But they have stated they will contact the Scottish Professional Football League over the issue.

Celtic will receive 508 tickets for the William Hill Premiership encounter on 29 November, which will be their first visit to Tynecastle since beating Hearts to the title in the final stages of last season amid a pitch invasion from some of their fans.

A Celtic statement read: “As supporters will know, our allocation for our forthcoming match against Heart of Midlothian at Tynecastle Stadium has been cut by 20 per cent, compared to our previous visit.

“There have been a variety of views expressed to the club from supporters in relation to accepting this allocation. Some groups representing travelling supporters explained to the club that their members did not wish to accept the tickets because of the reduced allocation.

“We have taken that into consideration and also raised their concerns with the home club, who have assured us that they have spoken to Police Scotland.

“Having carefully considered all of the circumstances, we can confirm we will accept the allocation of 508 tickets.

“We respect all views and opinions on this matter, and while we are concerned and disappointed at this reduction, and others across recent years, we feel it is important that the team has the backing of our fans within the stadium for an important match.

“We realise the difficulties such a reduction can cause and in light of our discussions with supporters, we can confirm that should any supporter who is successful in the ballot, but does not wish to accept this ticket, then this will NOT affect the away ticket record moving forward.

“We thank our fans for their continued support and can confirm that we will be discussing the matter further with both the home club and the SPFL.”

Celtic and Rangers formerly received the full Roseburn Stand for their supporters at Tynecastle, which resulted in an allocation of almost 3,500 tickets.

However, that figure was reduced to about 1,250 tickets in the 2021-22 season amid increased demand from home fans after the lockdown, and was further cut by about half.

Only Hibernian now get the full Roseburn Stand in a reciprocal agreement between the Edinburgh rivals.

Tynecastle has a capacity of about 20,000 but Hearts’ attendances are normally around 18,700 as a number of seats are not in use to create a barrier between the home and away fans.

Visiting clubs get about 800 tickets for games at Celtic Park, which has a 60,000 capacity.

#891. Borussia Dortmund's Felix Nmecha and the question of religion

Felix Nmecha's "Crowns down" celebration has drawn criticism from a Borussia Dortmund fan club, reopening debate over faith, inclusion and religious messaging in football.

Felix Nmecha's renewed use of the "Crowns down celebration" — where a crown is pretended to be removed from someone's head and placed at Jesus' feet — has sparked a reaction from Borussia Dortmund's official supporters' group.

"Faith does not justify exclusion. Faith does not justify division. Borussia Dortmund is a club for everyone," read a statement after the Bundesliga club beat Elversberg, a game in which Nmecha scored twice. Nmecha's first documented "Crowns down celebration" was at the 2026 World Cup, for which "The King's Return" campaign was launched.

"In the past, the the Borussia Dortmund supporters club has deliberately refrained from commenting on sports-related issues and the athletic performance of individual players. We remain committed to this approach," the statement continued.

"However, when it comes to our club's values, discrimination, and the question of what view of humanity is fostered within and around Borussia Dortmund, we cannot and will not remain silent."

The fan club states their issue is not with Nmecha being a devout Christian, but rather his public support for "The King's Return" campaign, which the supporters club said "gives us cause to reassess the situation."

This campaign, according to research by German public broadcaster ARD in the summer of 2026, was designed by the "Ballers in God" (BIG) network. BIG was founded in 2015 by footballer John Bostock, a devout Christian who wanted to create a community where professional footballers could strengthen each other in their faith, pray together, and read the Bible. In over a decade since, the BIG community has grown to nearly 800,000 followers on Instagram.

Nmecha issued a response on social media not long afterwards, writing:

"I've been told that my most recent goal celebration has led to some misunderstandings," Nmecha wrote.

"My message was never intended to spread intolerance, discrimination, or hatred in any form. As Christians, our message is one of love and respect for every person—regardless of where someone comes from, what they believe in, or what worldview they hold."

Reports suggest that both the board at Dortmund and Germany head coach Jürgen Klopp will speak to Nmecha on the matter in the coming days.

The fan club say their criticism is "directed at religious networks that, under the guise of faith, promote a worldview in which people are devalued or marginalized because of their sexual orientation, gender identity, lifestyle, or personal choices... When religious beliefs are used to deny people their dignity or equality, that is where our tolerance for intolerance ends."

Here, they are referring to the recent ARD investigation. That work revealed the homepage for "The King's Return" campaign featured a link to a live counseling chat run by US-based evangelical nonprofit Groundwire. During the investigations, counselors told reporters that abortion is "Satan's plan" and that homosexuality is a sin.

Borussia Dortmund's statement of core values commits the club to diversity, human rights, and inclusion regardless of gender, sexual orientation, faith, or background. The club's largest and most influential fan group also promotes progressive, anti-fascist, and inclusive values. It is also part of a wider fan landscape in Germany where club members are more involved in club decisions than in many other countries. This was evidenced when the club signed a deal with arms manufacturer Rheinmetall two years ago and in the case of Nmecha as well. When the midfielder signed for Dortmund in 2023, many of the club's fans protested because the player had previously shared or liked several transphobic and homophobic posts on his Instagram account. In response, Nmecha deleted some posts and instead issued a statement emphasizing "I do not discriminate against anyone."

Article 4 of German Basic Law guarantees that each individual is allowed to decide how strongly, why and which god to believe in. In football, players cannot display political, religious, or personal slogans, statements, or images on their jerseys, undershirts, or gear. However, physical gestures are allowed so long as they don't delay the game or antagonize the crowd.

The use of physical religious gestures has history in sports, as professor Paul Putz described in his book "The Spirit of the Game: American Christianity and Big-Time Sports". Putz describes how the the pioneers of the Christian athlete movement realized they: "could influence others to Christian ideals more effectively on the field than in the pulpit."

And yet, such gestures can also be at odds with the atmosphere of modern sports arenas, particularly football. In their book "Sports and Christianity: Historical and Contemporary Perspectives", Nick J. Watson and Andrew Parker explain how modern sport has become a substitute for traditional faith.

"Sport seduces the teeming 'global village'; it is the new opiate of the masses; it is one of the great modern experiences … Sport, for many, has replaced religion as a source of emotional catharsis and spiritual passion," they wrote.

With the 26-year-old Nmecha a key player for both club and country, the conversation around faith and football looks set to continue for some time yet.

#890. Moody: I felt ready to play after receiving Haka

Former England captain Lewis Moody joined England to receive the Haka ahead of their 37-12 victory over the All Blacks on Saturday; Moody fronted England's arrow-head formation for the pre-match tradition

Lewis Moody says he "felt ready to play" after he joined England to receive New Zealand's Haka, ahead of Maro Itoje's side's 37-12 victory over the All Blacks on Saturday.

Emotional scenes unfolded at Allianz Stadium, as Moody, who was diagnosed with motor neurone disease (MND) in 2025, walked arm-in-arm with Itoje onto the field.

New Zealand's players clapped as the former England captain took up position at the front of England's arrow-head formation - between Itoje and Ellis Genge - to accept the challenge of the Haka.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Moody, who won 71 international caps during his career, had presented England's players with their matchday shirts at their Pennyhill Park base on Friday, and revealed Ollie Chessum had jokingly urged him to stay on the pitch and chase down the first kick.

"I honestly felt ready to play," Moody told BBC Breakfast.

"When the lads were hugging me after the Haka, I was like: 'Right, I'm ready to go'."

"The night before, Ollie Chessum told me where they were going for the first kick-off.

"He was like: 'Mate, if you're up for it, you can chase it!'

"I was almost ready to take him up on that."

In support of Moody's Front Up to Motor Neurone Disease campaign, England's players wore boots as well as special warm-up and arrival kit with the campaign's logo printed on them.

The players also signed warm-up tops and match shirts, which were donated to the My Name'5 Doddie Foundation, a charity founded by the late Scotland international Doddie Weir that provides funds for MND research.

"I was really aware that this was something that I would never get to feel again and hadn't felt for over 15 years," Moody said.

"So, I wanted to try and fully take in the moment.

"When I got out there, Maro [Itoje] brought me out there and positioned me.

"Ellis [Genge] embraced me, the bundle of physical energy that he is. That's inspiring in itself, to feel the power that's emanating through his body.

"The noise was almost overwhelming. And then [I tried] to recentre myself and focus on the Haka, through the peripheral vision of the England team that fanned out in front of me.

"It just brought a huge smile, and brought back a lot of wonderful memories of playing with all my former team-mates."

He added: "It was really unique and I feel humbled to have been a part of it."

Front Up to MND are organising a series of coastal walk fundraisers on June 12 2027 to raise money for the My Name'5 Doddie Foundation.

"To have the response that it did and to have the support that it has is only good for the cause that I was there for, which is the Front Up campaign supporting My Name'5 Doddie Foundation, to raise as much money as possible, to have a serious impact on this disease," Moody said.

"We need more drugs that have a significant impact for patients. They are the breakthroughs that we're looking for and this campaign will get us near, if not over the line with that.

"But we need thousands, if not tens of thousands, hundreds of thousands of people to support and get involved.

"And hopefully, if you're a little bit inspired or if you just loved watching the game at the weekend, and everything that represented, and you fancied taking on a challenge, come and join us on June 12, walking the coast."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Asked whether Moody's presence motivated England, Seb Atkinson told Sky Sports News:

"Definitely, he came into the hotel last night and gave us some reflections on his career and some reflections on his diagnosis.

"It was really special to be a part of that. I think the lads really took it on board.

"Then to hear the noise of him coming out and taking part in our response to the Haka was really special.

"Also to see his family and his sons and speak to himself [Moody] in the changing rooms after, it just topped it off."

The Crystal Palace man hasn't lived up to previous seasons' form in 2026/27

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Having just experienced one of the best nights of his footballing life, Adam Wharton was not in the mood to dwell on a negative. Fresh from starring in Crystal Palace’s 1-0 victory over Rayo Vallecano in the Conference League final in May, Wharton was asked how he felt about missing out on England’s World Cup squad. The midfielder smiled, shrugged and shuffled in his chair before playing down his disappointment.

“That's just part of football. It was never a guarantee I was going to go. I knew that,” Wharton said. “I'm not going to sit here and cry about it… it's not the end of the world. I’m still young. Hopefully there's other tournaments and World Cups that I can go to in the future.”

A few months on, that remains an ambition for Wharton. Right now, though, he has more pressing things to worry about.

Wharton, like Crystal Palace as a whole, has endured a poor start to the season. His omission from Thomas Tuchel's latest England squad did not raise any eyebrows. With the January window set to open in just over six weeks, Wharton's suitors must ask themselves whether this is a mere blip or a sign of deeper problems.

There are mitigating factors behind his dip in form. The transition from Oliver Glasner to Pierre Sage was not smooth, culminating in the Frenchman's expected sacking. Wharton has not had a consistent partner in the engine room, with Daichi Kamada and Quentin Timber - two players with very different characteristics - taking turns alongside him.

When Dean Henderson was out injured earlier this season, Wharton was made captain. The armband appeared to weigh him down.

Wharton has also missed Ismaila Sarr and Jean-Philippe Mateta, Palace's two primary goal threats who have had disrupted starts to the campaign. Wharton's through-balls are most effective when they are aimed at players with the pace to run onto them. Yeremy Pino and Kamada, the wide forwards against Liverpool before the international break, are not ideal targets.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

For all that, Wharton himself would be the first to admit that his performances have been far below his usual standards. His confidence has deserted him. Not helped by a collective lack of compactness out of possession, Wharton has too often been overrun. His tendency to go to ground when attempting to win the ball back carries substantial risk, leaving him out of the game if the tackle is unsuccessful.

Most worrying is his reduced effectiveness with the ball. Data from analytics company Gradient Sports shows that only Elliot Anderson (107) and Jan Paul van Hecke (97) have attempted more line-breaking passes than Wharton, but the Palace man ranks joint-12th for line-breaking passes completed. His pass completion rate is a lowly 74%.

This has always been Wharton’s game. He has never been a safe distributor, preferring instead to put the ball at risk in the hope of creating something. Of Premier League midfielders who have played more than 100 minutes this season, only Vitaly Janelt (44.8%) has a higher percentage of passes played forward than Wharton (43.6%).

The trade-off was worth it for Palace last season, but when Wharton’s radar is slightly off, he becomes extremely wasteful. That raises an important question. The top clubs generally prize control in the centre of the park. Having the skill and vision to create chances via progressive passing is valuable, but so too is the ability to keep possession ticking over. If Wharton wants to take the next step in his career, that is something he needs to add to his game.

In the meantime, Wharton would benefit from having another body around him in midfield. Thomas Frank, who is expected to be Palace’s next manager, is likely to switch from a 3-4-3 formation to either a 4-3-3 or a 4-2-3-1. With both Timber and Kamada alongside him in the engine room, Wharton would be freer to focus on doing what he does best. If Palace can get Sarr back in the XI consistently, even better.

Wharton has not become a bad player overnight, but he is going through his first prolonged dip in form since moving to the Premier League. If Palace are to clamber out of relegation trouble, they need Wharton back to his best.

Greg Lea is a freelance football journalist who's filled in wherever FourFourTwo needs him since 2014. He became a Crystal Palace fan after watching a 1-0 loss to Port Vale in 1998, and once got on the scoresheet in a primary school game against Wilfried Zaha's Whitehorse Manor (an own goal in an 8-0 defeat).

#888. Dundee manager wanted to ‘crawl under a rock and hide’ after 8-0 home thrashing

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Dundee were obliterated by Hearts in their heaviest-ever home league defeat

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Steven Pressley revealed the embarrassment of Dundee’s 8-0 hammering by Hearts on Saturday left him wanting to “crawl under a rock and hide”.

The Dark Blues manager has shouldered full responsibility after his team suffered their heaviest-ever home league defeat.

Speaking as Dundee prepared to return to action at Hibernian on Tuesday, Pressley said: “It’s been a difficult 24-48 hours. There’s been a lot of hurt, a lot of embarrassment. As you can imagine, at times I’ve wanted to crawl under a rock and hide.

“It’s difficult on the back of such a disappointing result. But I will say this, I suffer a lot from vulnerability at times, but for some reason during difficult moments I seem to find strength from somewhere.

“I don’t know if it’s from my family, from messages that I’ve received, from my reading.

“But I’ve had to show strength, I have to support the players. I have to make sure we navigate our way out of what was a really embarrassing moment.

“We had a good meeting yesterday. We chatted a lot about the various aspects, and hopefully we can start responding to the disappointment.”

Pressley said he had feared a setback coming for Dundee – “not 8-0 but a disappointing performance” – because he had “sensed a little bit of subconscious complacency”.

The manager felt his team had been over-hyped by outsiders on the back of a start to the season in which they won five of their 12 matches before the international break.

“We’re nowhere near the levels that people keep telling us we are,” he stressed. “We’re not a good enough team not to do the hard yards. Our whole strength has been built on the cohesion of the team, the unity of the team, the aggressiveness of the team.

“And I think what Saturday did highlight is exactly what I’ve been saying. If we get lazy on the hard yards, we’re a very vulnerable team.

“We have to be at our absolute best to get results. If we fall below that, we’re nowhere near the levels that people have been telling us we’re at.”

Pressley said Saturday has to represent “a reset moment, a moment we can always come back to to help us become better”. Asked if he expected a positive response from his players at Easter Road just 72 hours on from their Hearts humbling, he said: “I don’t know.

“I know that they’re hurting. I know that they want to respond in the best possible way. That part I don’t question. I know how much it’s affected them.

“But we’ve not had a lot of time. I just hope we can bring some pride back to the football club with the right type of performance.”

#886. Megaspeed and the battle to go high-end Nvidia chips into China

Jensen Huang's affair with a suspected Chinese spy has shone a light on Megaspeed, the company she worked for. It is under investigation in the US for smuggling Nvidia chips into China, which it denies.

As Nvidia, one of the world's most valuable companies, grapples with CEO Jensen Huang's romantic relationship with an alleged Chinese spy, attention is turning to the much smaller company she worked for.

Alice H., the alleged spy, worked as an executive for Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center and AI computing company. It manages data center access, including for some major Chinese tech firms such as Alibaba.

According to Megaspeed's website as of November 2026, the company advertises itself as an "Nvidia cloud partner", saying it provides "computing power product services covering Nvidia's entire GPU product line." GPU stands for Graphic Processing Unit, a specialized electronic circuit that are in high demand for artificial intelligence (AI) applications, because they are designed to handle high numbers of parallel mathematical calculations. Megaspeed says it provides access for clients to Nvidia's advanced GB200 NVL72 ​computing system.

This type of firm is often referred to as a "neocloud". It buys Nvidia chips and computing power and then rents it out — in this case, at multiple sites across south-east Asia, to different companies. The US has set up strict export controls to prevent that Nvidia's high-performance chips end up in China, because it sees China as a competitor in the global AI race. It also does not want data centers made up of Nvidia chips to be owned by Chinese companies. It does, however, tolerate that data center compute with Nvidia chips be rented out to Chinese companies like Alibaba, and occasionally allows the export of Nvidia chips for specific purposes.

Megaspeed has bought billions of dollars worth of Nvidia's products in recent years and has been accused of breaching US export controls to divert Nvidia chips into China.

In December 2025, Bloomberg reported that the "once-obscure" Megaspeed had become the biggest buyer of Nvidia's chips in all of south-east Asia and that the US government was investigating its ownership structure and whether or not it was smuggling Nvidia chips into China.

At the same time, Singapore police began an investigation into whether or not Megaspeed had "violated local laws" without specifying which ones. Those investigations are believed to be still ongoing.

On December 23, 2025, Megaspeed strenuously denied any wrongdoing in a statement — which still appears as the first page for visitors to the company's website as of November 2026.

"There has been no evidence of any violations concerning the illicit transfer of chips or any illegal activities, and this demonstrates that we are a compliant and legitimate company," it said. "We operate fully within the bounds of all applicable export control regulations and maintain the highest standards of legal and ethical conduct."

The US government investigation began in 2024. The Commerce Department initially began looking into Megaspeed, but the US Justice Department has since taken over. According to the New York Times, this switch came about after an Nvidia executive directly contacted the Commerce Department about the investigation.

Megaspeed was founded in 2015 and was originally called 7Road International. It changed its name to Megaspeed in March 2023. It is owned by the Singapore-registered Swiftdata, which was set up in October 2023.

Its rise in prominence coincided with a sharp increase in assets, which increased from $33 million in 2023 to $3 billion in 2024.

Alice H., the woman accused of being a Chinese spy, had an affair with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. She is widely seen as an influential figurehead at Megaspeed. She also served as the company's managing director of Megaspeed for eight months in 2023.

The Financial Times reported on Monday that Alice H. leveraged her close access to Jensen Huang and Nvidia to pitch AI chips deals to Chinese investors.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The newspaper said that in early 2025, Alice H. sought investment in China for a data center project in south-east Asia, and cited their easy access to Nvidia chips and close relationship with Alibaba.

Alibaba lent money to Megaspeed in June 2024, via subsidiaries. It has remained Megaspeed's largest client, according to reporting by the Financial Times.

In December 2025, Nvidia said its own inquiry into Megaspeed had found no evidence of chips being diverted and that the company was fully owned and operated outside of China, with no Chinese shareholders. The company told Bloomberg at the time that it had visited Megaspeed's facilities on multiple occasions and had seen nothing untoward.

Megaspeed is one of several companies accused of smuggling Nvidia's chips into China or finding ways to give Chinese companies access to them.

Nvidia's high-performance chips are seen as essential for companies looking for the most advanced form of supercomputing to use and develop various AI applications.

Back in 2022, the Biden Administration began severely restricting the sale of the US's most advanced chips to China, part of the two countries' growing rivalry to achieve AI dominance.

However, an illegal smuggling and underground network was soon set up, with many vendors operating to get the chips into China and selling them on to companies there.

In December 2025, US authorities shut down the operations of Hao Global, a US-based shell company with links to China which plead guilty to smuggling Nvidia chips to China.

In June 2026, Taiwanese government agencies raided the offices of Super Micro Computer as part of an investigation into the smuggling of Nvidia chips to China.

While export restrictions have been eased significantly under the Trump administration, there are still significant blocks and restrictions on the most advanced Nvidia chips.

In December 2025, the Trump administration approved several Chinese companies to buy or handle advanced Nvidia H200 chips, a move that sparked significant concern among the US security establishment.

However, that deal has not led to a significant flow of Nvidia chips moving legally to China, amid strict US licencing controls and official reluctance from Beijing to publicly promote Nvidia chips to the detriment of its own alternatives.

#885. Why is Kai Havertz always offside for Arsenal this season?

The Gunners' forward just can’t seem to time his runs this season

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Injuries hardly aided Kai Havertz last season. Regardless, his standing within the Arsenal squad was evidently high. As the Gunners went in search of a first Premier League title for 22 years, he was the one who Mikel Arteta turned to during the run-in, despite Viktor Gyokeres’ big money summer arrival from Sporting CP.

In the Champions League final showdown with Paris Saint-Germain, Arteta again called on the German, and was duly rewarded as he fired the north London side in front with just six minutes on the clock. Unsurprisingly, Havertz remains the Gunners’ first-choice frontman, even if a return of three goals in the opening 10 league outings is hardly a great return.

Saying that, there is more to Havertz’s game than just putting the ball in the back of the net. The Germany international’s selflessness and impressive link-up play is a key reason behind his continued selection ahead of a more natural No. 9 in Gyokeres. Arteta wants his leading forward to drop deeper to bring teammates into play, dragging markers out of position to open up space for the wingers to exploit.

And yet, his offside numbers resemble that of former AC Milan and Italy icon Filippo Inzaghi. “That lad must have been born offside,” Sir Alex Ferguson once quipped about the Italian, who addressed the comments to FourFourTwo back in 2023. In the modern day, Ferguson’s quote would be applicable to Havertz.

After all, Havertz has been flagged offside 15 times in the Premier League this season. It’s almost double that of the player in second for this metric, with Dominic Calvert-Lewin (8) his closest competitor. He’s been penalised for being in the wrong place more times than four Premier League teams.

For context, Bukayo Saka was caught offside more times (14) than any other player in the 2025/26 Premier League campaign. Havertz did so on just three occasions. “Certainly, it’s far too many,” Arteta said of the number of times Arsenal have been caught offside in the Premier League this season following the 1-0 win over Hull City prior to the international break.

So, for a player who is renowned for dropping deep in order to help his side in the final third, why has Kai Havertz been flagged offside so often this season?

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Well, for a start, Arsenal are a team that see more of the ball than the majority of the other 19 teams in England’s top tier. Only Manchester City (65.9%) and Tottenham Hotspur (63%) have managed a greater possession share than the defending champions (59.8%) in the Premier League. A return of 1379 successful final third passes is the second-most. So, too, is 31 total through balls.

It’s only natural that the amount of final third passes would result in a higher number of offsides. When teams attack an opposition backline, the side on the back foot will understandably work harder to catch you offside.

Who is to blame then? Obviously Havertz is at fault but he’s making the requisite runs to try and get in on goal.

According to Opta, only Fulham’s Gonzalo Garcia (145) and Manchester United forward Bryan Mbeumo (141) have made more in-behind high-intensity runs than Havertz (125) in the Premier League this season.

Despite his gangly appearance, the former Chelsea man is deceptively quick off the mark.

He’s playing off the shoulder of the last defender, and if those in support were prepared to release the ball a little quicker, then his runs would be capitalised upon to great effect. However, his teammates have been guilty of taking an extra touch, or taking a split-second longer to play the pass for Havertz. As such, his momentum takes him beyond the last man, meaning he either needs to check his run late, and a chance breaks down, or stray offside.

Of course, as things stand, Arsenal are hardly faltering domestically as a result of Havertz’s fondness for the flag. Admittedly, though, 15 goals scored doesn’t make for great reading - it’s level with Ipswich Town. And there will come a moment where these ill-timed runs and passes do have a detrimental impact on the team. “Yes, it’s something to improve,” Arteta added following the Hull triumph. It’s an issue that he concedes requires focus.

Yet Arsenal’s relentlessness combined with a watertight backline that has shipped just five goals means they are managing to get the job done.

Six of their 10 league wins have been by a single goal. A little more synchronisation between Havertz and the ammo suppliers would go a long way to give Arsenal more breathing space in their title defence.

Ben is a freelance football expert with over 15 years of experience in the field, ranging from stats, to betting, to transfer analysis, to news, and everything in between. Having departed esteemed football stats website WhoScored.com in 2025, he has been touring the freelance circuit, and has been featured on The Guardian, The Independent, Sky Sports, The Premier League, TNT Sports, ESPN, Squawka and talkSPORT, among others.

#884. Home nations expect Fifa to be in ‘different place’ by time of 2035 World Cup

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The football associations of England, Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales will be working alongside Fifa in hosting the tournament

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

The home nations expect Fifa to be in a “different place” by the time they host the Women’s World Cup in 2035 after withdrawing their support for president Gianni Infantino earlier this year.

The joint bid from England, Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales was approved at the Fifa Congress on Monday, although it was the sole bidder to host the 48-team tournament and was voted through by acclamation.

The tournament will be the first World Cup to be held in the UK since England hosted the men’s World Cup in 1966, but it comes just months after the chair of the English FA, Debbie Hewitt, demanded an independent investigation into Infantino’s scrapped World Cup sell-off plan and the Folarin Balogun affair, as well calls for further Fifa reform.

Infantino has retained the support required for re-election in March but cannot continue beyond 2031, and the FA’s director of women’s football Sue Day believes there will be significant change within Fifa as the home nations prepare to work alongside the governing body on staging the World Cup in 2035.

There have already been some challenges, with Fifa reportedly demanding tax-free status from ticket sales and broadcast and commercial partnerships, something that the UK government has not allowed when previously hosting major events such as the 2012 Olympics and will not offer to Uefa when they stage Euro 2028.

“There are two separate issues here, the concerns around the Fifa leadership and their proposals, and then this World Cup,” Day said on Monday.

“We very much want today to be about the excitement of this World Cup and we didn't want those concerns to get in the way of us trying to land the opportunity to put on this amazing tournament that we think can change the world of football.

“By the time the tournament comes around, lots of things will have changed. We expect Fifa to be in a different place.

“We know that there is a brilliant team there right now, led by Jill Ellis [former USA manager, now Fifa’s Chief Football Officer], leading women’s football and we're really looking forward to working with them on developing the tournament.”

Day also said that the home nations hope to have a “strong influence” on the pricing of the tournament. Fifa were accused of “betrayal” and price gouging when the ticket prices were revealed for last summer’s men’s World Cup in North American last summer but tickets for the 2027 Women’s World Cup in Brazil will go on sale for as little as £4 next month.

But Fifa is targeting revenues of $4bn when it stages the first 48-team World Cup in 2031, in the United States, Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica, and will be setting similar targets for the England, Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales bid.

“At the moment, the model is absolutely that Fifa decides those things,” Day said. “We will hope to be able to have a really strong influence on some of that because we know our audiences best.

“It’s going to be really important to get the pricing right. We all know that we need to show the commercial viability of women’s football, and we want this to be an accessible tournament.”

A 48-team Women’s World Cup would see the UK will host 104 matches across 39 days in 2035, in the largest single-sport event ever to be staged in the country, and Day said success for the tournament will be judged on its potential to transform society as well as what happens on the pitch.

“This is genuinely once in a lifetime, once in a generation,” Day said. “There wouldn’t have been a World Cup on this soil since 1966, which would be nearly 70 years away.

“And so I think just collectively, I want us to grasp the opportunity of this moment and really build towards it and think of it as, it will be the most amazing tournament, but it's [also] a catalyst for growth and inspiration and something to springboard from.

“I think we can change the world a little bit with the tournament and we should aim that high. Why wouldn't we aim that high?”

#883. John Toshack on Bill Shankly, Liverpool and an extraordinary football career

Join The Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation plus sign you up to our newsletter.
