#770. Ayanna Howard thinks ‘everyone has to be part of’ building ethical AI tools

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Robotics researcher Ayanna Howard sees artificial-intelligence tools as an equalizer. Credit: Emma Parker Photography

Rebooting the Machines: A New Human Vision for Artificial Intelligence Ayanna Howard Broadleaf (2026)

As artificial-intelligence tools upend the graduate job market, it might seem that there’s little for educators to be optimistic about. But AI and robotics pioneer Ayanna Howard, who is the president of Spelman College, a historically Black women’s university in Atlanta, Georgia, sees promise ahead.

Howard’s career has ranged from developing autonomous robotic systems at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory to serving as dean of the college of engineering at Ohio State University. She is a co-founder of Zyrobotics, a company that creates educational technologies for children who need extra support, and academic co-lead of Black in Robotics, an organization dedicated to making the robotics field more inclusive.

In her book Rebooting the machines, Howard explains that the dangers of AI are real. Yet AI tools can improve people’s quality of life and create job opportunities — if humanity implements guard rails. She spoke to Nature about why she tells her students to embrace the technology, albeit with healthy scepticism.

I consider myself a realistic optimist. I’m positive about the possibilities of AI tools, but I realize that not everyone thinks the same way as I do — including some AI developers and companies in this space. We still need to do something to turn that optimistic viewpoint into reality.

If all types of individuals — those from various socio-economic backgrounds, races, genders and nationalities, and those that have disabilities, for example — all become part of the AI ecosystem, tools can be personalized. For instance, in health care, I want AI tools that are trained on my body composition, taking into account my age and the fact that I’m female. I don’t want a general model that was trained on men.

Honestly, I’m optimistic about jobs. AI tools make knowledge much more accessible. For smart individuals who have not been trained as, say, a computer scientist, AI is an equalizer.

My advice is to have a healthy scepticism towards AI, but also to work out how to use these tools in your discipline and for your passions. Jobs are changing. For students starting university this year, I guarantee that when they graduate, the jobs available to them will be different to those that exist now.

I think that there is some fear, frankly, because some recent graduates don’t have jobs thanks to AI models accelerating the eradication of early-career roles. But the graduates who do get hired are those who know how to work with the AI tools that companies are throwing at them.

The ones that some people call soft skills, although I call them hard skills because AI models can’t replicate them. One of them is human curiosity, which leads to creativity. Also, people are really good at learning things for the first time, whereas AI needs tonnes of data to work anything out. That means humans are really good at dealing with anomalies.

Robots can be useful educational tools for children who have extra support needs.Credit: BSIP/UIG/Getty

The other element is that many jobs still rely on human connection. AI tools are pretty useful for diagnosis in health care. But we still want a human to interpret the AI output and interact with us. Those jobs are going to be difficult to replace.

Studies have shown that the current generation of young people report high levels of loneliness, and yet they’re also more connected than previous generations. I think that at some point they will say, ‘you know what? I don’t like being lonely. I need human connection’. But if people feel that AI is making them less lonely — although there is evidence that it isn’t — there is a risk that they will take a long time to come to that realization.

The other risk is that people begin to trust AI tools too much. Because AI models are getting so good, there is a tendency not to question them. For example, if an AI tool used in health care tells people something incorrect and they don’t examine it, that could be disastrous.

The cost of hardware has gone down, and the time needed for a robot to learn what we call the action space — I see something, I work out how to do something and then I am able to actually do it physically — has shortened. That’s what’s required to operate in the real world.

You can’t ‘control–alt–delete’ harm to a human. With a virtual AI tool, if it completes a task, it’s not doing anything physically. (Although, as AI agents become more sophisticated, there’s a question of how much longer that will be the case.) Currently, a human still has to say ‘yes’, or confirm or click something to initiate a behaviour. When an AI model controls a physical system, you don’t necessarily have that feedback loop. That is a very risky scenario.

One answer is to collect more data. There are communities that don’t give their data to organizations training AI models because they know that their information could be used against them. But for applications that involve high risk but high return, we have to have a conversation about it. When a company tests a drug, people are willing to volunteer to take it and provide their data, because the benefits outweigh the risks. Can we do the same thing for some AI applications?

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03721-9

#769. Spurs 'a match for anyone' as win at Man City boosts European hopes

Spurs secure famous win as Man City falter again

Dreams of reaching the Women's Champions League may have seemed fanciful for Tottenham Hotspur when the season began.

The Women's Super League has an established big four, and big-spending London City Lionesses were the side making the most obvious play to disrupt that dominance.

But a hugely impressive and deserved win at Manchester City on Sunday afternoon proves Spurs are a team on the up, and the table shows they remain firmly in top-three contention.

Two late goals secured a 3-1 win at Joie Stadium, but this was no smash-and-grab job. Spurs were more dynamic than sluggish City, pressing them into submission.

They restricted their hosts' stellar attack to precious few chances and took the ones they created.

"When we are on our game, we can be a match for anyone," Spurs manager Martin Ho said in his post-match media conference.

"It gives us confidence - but it is just one game."

Man City beaten by Spurs and miss chance to go top of WSL

Victory kept Spurs, whose highest finish in the WSL is fifth, firmly in the mix this time.

They are fifth again, but just three points behind London City Lionesses who occupy the final European place as the league heads into a last international break of 2026.

Chelsea lead the way from Manchester City, with Manchester United one point ahead of Tottenham, who in turn sit handily clear of their sixth-placed north London rivals Arsenal.

The big four are therefore all present in the top six. London City are right there, too, and Spurs, with six wins from 11 games so far, are gamely pressing their own case.

What made Sunday's win and performance from Tottenham even more impressive is how dreadful their recent record against Manchester City had been.

Tottenham had lost six of their previous seven away matches against City in all competitions, averaging over four goals conceded per defeat.

Last season City won this fixture 5-2 with Khadija Shaw scoring a 13-minute hat-trick, the quickest in WSL history.

Shaw's early goal on Sunday, her 16th in league matches versus Spurs, could easily have started a landslide.

That was expected. City had won each of their past 17 WSL home games, including all 10 in 2026 â until Tottenham tore up the script.

The outcome means Manchester City, beaten at Chelsea in their previous outing, have suffered consecutive league losses for the first time since January 2025.

Spurs have rediscovered form after losing all three league games in October while conceding 14 goals

Tottenham's victory came down to Ho's brave tactics and his team's superb execution of them.

After going behind, they pressed City constantly, forcing errors and creating chances. That tenacity won them countless one-on-ones, with City unable or unwilling to play over the press.

After her goal, Shaw was rendered anonymous by the hard work and close marking of centre-backs Toko Koga and Amanda Nilden.

Down the right, Kirsty Hanson dominated Carlotta Wamser, could have been awarded a penalty and provided the low cross for Cathinka Tandberg's equaliser.

In midfield, Drew Spence pulled all the strings and covered the entire pitch. At 34, she is perhaps playing the best football of her career and deserved her assist for the winner. After Matilda Vinberg put Spurs in front, several players ran to celebrate with Spence.

"When you come into this, you wonder if it will go against you, but the players were outstanding," said Ho.

"We haven't won here in so long, so we know it will be a tough game, but I have belief in my team when we are on song. I thought we were outstanding - we worked every blade of grass."

Spurs are clearly capable of taking the game to anyone in the league and have now scored 28 WSL goals this season, with only Chelsea and London City having more.

In the second half they adapted to City sending on such fluid attacking threats as Mary Fowler, Kerstin Casperij and Beth Mead.

They lifted the gas from the press, applying it more sparingly, and were solid in defence.

It shows that Ho has learned painful lessons from the past - whether from Spurs' poor record against City, including two five-goal losses in 2025-26, or conceding six to Chelsea and London City back to back in October.

"We have maybe been naive at times and I own that, so we are more reserved," Ho said of his tactical approach. "It was managing that, and the players' communication was excellent."

City were limited to fleeting chances. Jade Rose blasting over after keeper Lize Kop parried a Lauren Hemp free-kick was as close as they came to a second goal, and those were their first shots after a 50-minute drought.

When Spurs got their late chances through the hard work of Vinberg, they could strike for three points.

Vinberg had quite the rollercoaster afternoon. She was initially named on the bench but was promoted to the starting XI 15 minutes before kick-off as Olivia Holdt was suffering stomach cramps.

Perhaps unprepared, she gave away the ball playing out of defence leading to City's opener. But she grew into the game, scored Spurs' second goal and set up Jess Naz for the third.

It was a great moment for Naz, on her 100th WSL appearance of a career that has been disrupted by injury.

Spurs are back in Manchester before Christmas, visiting United on 20 December.

There will be real hope of a positive result as they press their way into contention for what would be a historic achievement of a top-three finish.

#768. Will Smith, Jada Pinkett Smith Step Out For Rare Family Outing

Will Smith and Jada Pinkett Smith enjoyed a multi-generational family outing with their kids Jaden, 28, and Willow, 26, and their moms Adrienne Banfield-Norris and Caroline Bright in Malibu.

Now this is a story all about how the Smith family had a special day out.

Will Smith and Jada Pinkett Smith enjoyed a rare public outing with their kids Jaden Smith, 28, and Willow Smith, 26, as they stepped out to visit Soho House’s Little Beach House Malibu in Malibu, Calif., on Nov. 21.

And it was a multi-generational family affair, with Will and Jada’s moms Caroline Bright and Adrienne Banfield-Norris, respectively, also tagging along for the outing at the oceanfront social club.

While the occasion appeared casual, the Smith brood didn’t slack on the fashion, with the family all making a statement with their looks.

Will, 58, sported a bright red zip-up, white T-shirt and jeans, which he accessorized with a white baseball hat. Jada, 55, meanwhile, rocked a chic black button-up shirt under a black leather jacket, along with dark grey trousers. The Girls Trip actress paired the look with red shoes and a black handbag.

As for the former couple’s kids, Willow donned a long green patterned coat over a pair of beige pants and boots, while Jaden kept it classic with a white zip-up hoodie.

And the family matriarchs made sure to show who’s in charge as Adrienne, 73, wore a navy sweater over camouflage pants and Caroline, 89, rocked a black-and-white printed ensemble.

Though Will and Jada—who quietly separated in 2016—have maintained a rather low profile in recent years, they have stepped out on multiple occasions to publicly show their support for their kids.

In June, the pair were joined by Willow, Adrienne and Will’s son Trey—whom he shares with ex Sheree Zampino—for a joint appearance at Paris Fashion Week to attend Christian Louboutin’s Menswear Spring/Summer 2027 show. After all, Jaden is the brand’s men’s creative director.

During the trip to the fashion capital, the pair enjoyed a night out with Jaden, linking arms as they stepped out for dinner.

The Paris outing came five months after Will and Jada reunited to support Jaden when he debuted his first collection with Christian Louboutin at Paris Fashion Week in January.

Though it’s been over a decade since the Bad Boys actor and Red Table Talk alum separated, Jada—who publicly revealed the breakup in 2023—shared that she and Will don’t plan on filing for divorce in the future.

As she told NBC News in Oct. 2023, “I made a promise that there will never be a reason for us to get a divorce.”

For a look back at Will and Jada’s relationship over the years, keep reading…

Will Smith and Jada Pinkett Smith were all smiles at the Devil in a Blue Dress premiere in 1995.

Have you ever seen anything more '90s glam than this? The couple posed together in 1997, the year they got married.

Jada was styling more than just a trendy silver coat in this 1998 red carpet photo—she was also showing off her baby bump in a sleek black dress. The couple's son Jaden Smith was born on July 8, 1998.

During Jada's second pregnancy with daughter Willow Smith in 2000, Will couldn't help but to cradle the actress' baby belly at a celebrity boxing match in Los Angeles.

Hats off to the couple who never cease to show up on a red carpet in style. Here they were together at Hollywood's Kodak Theater in 2005.

Jada ignored the old superstition of never wearing to black to a wedding as she and Will headed to Katie Holmes and Tom Cruise's 2006 nuptials in Rome.

The kids were here in London with Will and Jada on the red carpet at The Karate Kid premiere in 2010.

Orange you glad to see this picture of Will and Jada together? The pair got cozy during an event in New York City in 2010.

Willow, Jaden, Will and Jada posed together in a family shot at the Toronto International Film Festival in 2012.

Jada dazzled in green as she and Will arrived at the 2016 Golden Globe Awards at the Beverly Hilton Hotel.

Everyone was all smiles for a family vacation after making a quick pit stop at the 2018 World Cup.

In 2020, the couple addressed Jada's alleged affair with August Alsina.

Admitting she and August had an "entanglement" while she and Will were separated, she explained, "It was a relationship. I was in a lot of pain and I was very broken. In the process of that relationship I definitely realized you can't find happiness outside of yourself. Luckily enough, you and I were also going through a process of healing in a much different manner."

During the 2022 Academy Awards, Will slapped host Chris Rock over a joke the comedian made about Jada's shaved head.

After the slap, Will resigned from the Academy of Motion Picture Arts & Sciences and was banned from its events for 10 years. He also apologized to Chris, calling the slap "unacceptable" and noting "there is no part of me that thinks that was the right way to behave in that moment."

In October 2023, Jada revealed she and Will had been separated for seven years, including the six leading up to the 2022 Oscars.

"We're still figuring it out," Jada told People. "We've been doing some really heavy-duty work together. We just got deep love for each other and we are going to figure out what that looks like for us."

#767. IFA 'positive' over upgrades needed for World Cup

Windsor Park would require 5,000 additional seats to host games at the 2035 World Cup

The Irish Football Association's director of women's football Angela Platt said the organisation is "still working through" plans with the Northern Ireland government to ensure there is funding available to make the necessary upgrades to Windsor Park in time for the 2035 World Cup.

It was confirmed on Monday that Northern Ireland, England, Scotland and Wales, the only bidders for the tournament in nine years' time, had been ratified as co-hosts.

Of the 19 venues proposed by the 'All Together' bid, Belfast's Windsor Park is the sole stadium in Northern Ireland, but would require an additional 5,000 seats to its current capacity of 18,500 as well as changes to the pitch and floodlights.

"We're obviously working with our government partners who've committed their support to help us do that, and we'll continue our endeavours to make sure that we work towards that," Platt told BBC NI's Stephen Watson.

"We know that the Northern Ireland Executive has given a commitment to back us and do whatever they can to support us in our endeavours to make sure we're ready for that hosting of the Women's World Cup in 2035.

"We have a few years to make sure we work through that."

Northern Ireland was involved in a similar bid to host games at Euro 2028, but plans for fixtures in Belfast at that tournament fell through when the government said it would not provide funding to redevelop Casement Park in the required timescale.

Platt said that "was in the past" and that the organisation were focused on the work required to avoid any repeat.

"We're still working towards making sure that it does happen and we're positive. We know that the work is there to make sure that it happens," she added.

"It's obviously disappointing when something that people work so hard to put together doesn't come to fruition, but certainly that's in the past for us.

"From our perspective, working for women's football, this is a great opportunity for Northern Ireland to get behind this and actually make sure that we do everything we can to host our Women's World Cup games here."

UK to host 2035 Women's World Cup, Fifa confirms

Plans to increase Windsor Park capacity to 23,750

There is no guarantee that, even as co-hosts, there would an automatic qualification spot for Northern Ireland.

The side last qualified for a major tournament at Euro 2022 and Platt believes bringing the World Cup to the country has the potential to "inspire a new generation".

"I think it can have a huge impact. We've always been blessed that we have had our women's team involved in the Women's Euros in 2022, and through my role, I get to visit other nations hosting tournaments such as this," she said.

"I was in Sydney for the Women's World Cup (2023) and obviously saw the impact hosting a tournament like that had in New Zealand and Australia, and likewise for the Euros in England and Switzerland recently.

"That impact is significant. It's the growth of the game, it's the engagement, it's the legacy. So much positivity can come out of hosting major tournaments and we're excited to play our part in this and it can only have benefits for Northern Ireland in general."

#764. Aspyn Ovard Details Decision to Have Baby No. 3 Amid Daughter's Cancer

The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives: Orange County star Aspyn Ovard shared why she decided to have a third baby after her daughter Cove, 7, was diagnosed with cancer: "Being pregnant saved my life."

Aspyn Ovard is shedding light on her motherhood journey.

Over a week after the Secret Lives of Mormon Wives: Orange County star shared her daughter Cove’s terminal cancer diagnosis on the Hulu series premiere, she explained why she decided to grow her family and have a third baby with then-husband Parker Ferris amid their eldest daughter’s health battle.

“I didn’t want my other child to grow up alone,” Ovard—mom to daughters Lola, 5, and Elle, 2, with Ferris—shared in a Nov. 21 YouTube vlog, answering a fan’s question about her decision to have more kids. “I did decide to have another baby. I did do it on kind of a crazy timeline.”

“It was a lot to be doing all of that with everything we were going through, but I just knew that that was what was right for our family,” she continued. “I didn’t want a really big age gap, so that was something that I put myself through and did for my family and for my daughters.”

And although it was difficult, the YouTuber emphasized that she doesn’t regret her choice.

“I have never felt like I shouldn’t have done it on that timeline,” she stressed. “I’m very glad that I did.”

And while the 30-year-old and Ferris were in the midst of navigating Cove’s diagnosis at the time, Ovard noted that being pregnant ultimately made her stronger.

“That was the one thing I could focus on,” she recalled, “and the one thing that was in my control.”

Though the reality star admitted that it’s difficult to discuss that time, she shared that pregnancy “kept me going.”

“I do think that being pregnant saved my life,” Ovard continued. “I don’t know how I would have had the strength to keep going and stay here if I was not growing that baby, so that also was a huge reason why I felt like I needed to do that in that time.”

The social media personality welcomed daughter Elle in 2024, announcing the birth of her third baby on the same day she filed for divorce from Ferris.

While revealing Cove’s cancer diagnosis for the first time on the premiere episode of the Mormon Wives: OC, Ovard shared that her marriage to Ferris was already struggling when the former couple learned of their daughter’s diagnosis.

“My marriage was nowhere near in a place to be able to make it through something like this,” she said during an emotional confessional. “We weren't even going to make it through before this happened.”

For a closer look at the cast of Secret Lives of Mormon Wives: Orange County, keep reading…

After many ups and downs, Jen Affleck—who is pregnant with her and Zac Affleck's fourth baby—officially filed for divorce from her husband of seven years, E! News confirmed Nov. 4.

Aspyn Ovard, who filed for divorce from Parker Ferris in 2024 after eight years of marriage, is currently in a throuple relationship with married couple Billy Davis and Bri Davis.

Following her divorce from Cory Althoff, podcaster Bobbi Althoff started dating Tyler Hawkins, who plays a special role in Secret Lives of Mormon Wives: Orange County.

"He styles me, that’s how he supports me,” she told E! News in May 2026, adding that the basketball player, "picks out my outfits every day. He styles me every day for the show. It’s great."

However, Hawkins confirmed in a November 2026 TikTok that the duo had split two months prior.

Despite ongoing relationship speculation, Salomé Andrea and Aaron Brimhall are still going strong as they prepare to welcome their third baby together. The duo, who married in 2012, welcomed twins Luca and Rue in 2018 and daughter named Shiloh in 2026.

McCall DaPron—the sister of Mormon Wives' Mayci Neeley—shares four kids with husband Kirk DaPron, who she wed in 2011.

Ashleigh Pease and Nate Pease are rock solid after over a decade of marriage. "This 13th year together is one that has felt full circle!" she wrote on Instagram in September. "A season of fruits. Comfort. The happiest milestones."

Madison Bontempo and Kyler Steven Fisher, who wed in 2013, have been open about the highs and lows of their relationship. "Kyler and I aren’t perfect," she wrote on Instagram in October. "We’ve had arguments. We’ve had hard seasons. We’ve had moments we wish we could take back. And we’re not afraid to admit that."

But, she added, "Those moments aren’t our whole story. There’s also laughter, friendship, forgiveness, growth, five beautiful children, a million memories, and a love that has continued to evolve through every season of our lives."

Avery Woods and David Woods, parents to Ziggy and Stevie, are still feeling the love after a decade of marriage. As she simply put it, "my forever + always."

#763. From conceding seven to Hull heroics - how Tzolakis recovered to defy Brighton

McBurnie stoppage-time double earns Hull win over 10-man Brighton

Hull boss Sergej Jakirovic used one word to describe the performance of his goalkeeper Konstantinos Tzolakis in Sunday's 2-0 Premier League win against Brighton.

"Unbelievable," he told Match of the Day.

"Especially after the international break, which was very difficult for him."

Tzolakis' previous outing had been for Greece against the Netherlands in the Uefa Nations League, where he and his side were humbled 7-0 by the hosts in Amsterdam.

Nine days later, his contribution to the Tigers' first league victory since 29 August was every bit as important as that of striker Oli McBurnie, who netted both goals in second-half stoppage time against the second-placed Seagulls.

Tzolakis made a series of top saves to keep the highest scorers in the top flight at bay and, when Brighton full-back Costinha was sent off in the 89th minute for a second bookable offence, the hosts seized their opportunity to clinch only their third win following their Premier League return.

McBurnie said the 24-year-old stopper had "kept Hull in a few games" this season and the club were "lucky to have him", while Tzolakis told Sky Sports: "We are a unit and a team.

"We play for each other. We showed a good team effort and we deserved the three points."

McBurnie scores stoppage-time double as Hull stun Brighton

How 'outstanding' Tzolakis kept Brighton at bay

With the opportunity to move three points behind leaders Arsenal, Brighton looked most likely to score for long spells of Sunday's game, but just could not find a way past former Olympiacos goalkeeper Tzolakis, who joined Hull in August for a reported Â£20m fee.

He got down to make a vital block early on to deny Diego Gomez, who had slid in to meet a low cross from the left wing. It was the first of several occasions the Paraguay international would be frustrated in front of goal.

Tzolakis then raced out spreadeagled to foil Georginio Rutter with an outstretched left hand - a stop that BBC Radio 5 Live pundit and former striker Clinton Morrison described as "Peter Schmeichel-esque", referring to the legendary Denmark keeper.

Second-half efforts from distance by Pascal Gross and Lewis Dunk were dealt with, too.

Yasin Ayari went close with a thumping strike against the bar and when Brighton substitute Charalampos Kostoulas pounced on a short backpass to go through one-on-one, Tzolakis got a hand on his Greece team-mate's shot and Regan Slater was back on the goalline to head the ball to safety.

Former Liverpool midfielder Danny Murphy, a pundit on Sunday's Match of the Day, said: "We saw again how important Tzolakis is for Hull. He had one of those days where he was always in the right place at the right time.

"When you are a Hull player and you see the kind of saves Tzolakis made when he spread himself and kept it out with his foot, you start thinking that it could be your day.

"It happens a lot in football and, on the flip side, Brighton will have been thinking, 'are we ever going to score here?'."

Hull made a superb start to the campaign after being promoted via the Championship play-offs in May.

They followed victories against Manchester United and Coventry with a draw against Aston Villa - all without conceding a goal.

The Tigers had not won since that 1-0 success at Coventry until beating Brighton - but they are one of four top-flight sides still unbeaten at home and have not lost any fixture by more than a one-goal margin.

They lost 1-0 to champions Arsenal before the international break and Scotland forward McBurnie told Match of the Day: "We know we can make it difficult for the top teams in the league and we've proved that in the past two games.

"We want to make it as difficult as we can for teams to come here and make the MKM Stadium a tough place to come. It's proving that way so far, so long may it continue."

#762. Germany news: Parliament agrees on debt-laden 2027 budget

The budget committee in the Bundestag worked into the night to sign off on next year's spending plans. These include levels of new debt only eclipsed once, at the height of the COVID pandemic.

These updates have been closed. Below, you can review our collection of news and analysis on stories from or relating to Germany from Friday, November 13.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz got a birthday cake at the UN climate summit in Turkey this week. But he wasn't there to eat it. Meanwhile, in Berlin, climate activists marked his 71st birthday on Friday with a symbolic chocolate cake. Their message: they too want to reach that age on a livable planet.

Fridays for Future is taking its demands to German streets. Demonstrations were planned in more than 70 German cities on Friday, November 13.

Under the slogan "Pay your climate debt," protesters in the German capital demanded more funding for climate protection and adaptation in developing countries, alongside a global phase-out of coal, oil and gas.

Germany provided €4.7 billion ($5.2 billion) in federal budget funds for international climate financing in 2025 — below its €6 billion pledge.

But the protest movement is no longer drawing the crowds it once did. In September 2019, Fridays for Future mobilized an estimated 1.4 million people across Germany. Five years later, that figure fell to around 75,000 at a comparable nationwide strike.

This comes as broader youth frustration with German politics grows. "I don't feel addressed by the chancellor unfortunately," Kim, a protester in Berlin, told DW.

From military service to affordable housing and climate policy, younger Germans are questioning whether their concerns are being heard.

A recent nationwide poll found that 82% of Germans believe politicians do not adequately represent young people's interests. Among 18- to 34-year-olds, just 5% trust Merz's conservatives to champion their concerns, compared with 3% for their Social Democratic coalition partners.

Merz is not the first German chancellor to miss a UN climate summit. And smaller demonstrations do not necessarily mean young Germans care less about climate change. But the contrast is striking: while the climate movement struggles to mobilize, dissatisfaction among younger voters extends well beyond environmental policy.

Julian Reichelt, formerly the editor-in-chief of Germany's top-selling tabloid Bild, says he was the target of an arson attack after his car was set on fire and largely destroyed in Berlin.

Now editor-in-chief of the right-wing online portal Nius that he co-founded, Reichelt said the arson attack took place in the Charlottenburg district of the German capital overnight.

Police confirmed the car was intentionally set alight, saying a passerby reported it shortly after 2 a.m. that morning. However, they did not name a suspect or potential personal motive at first, saying only that the fire department responded and extinguished the fire.

"It is completely clear that this was a targeted attack," Reichelt said, calling it an "attempt at intimidation against new free media that stand up against this left-wing extremism."

Similar arson attacks several years ago targeted cars belonging to a columnist for another Berlin newspaper, B.Z., with a left-wing group claiming responsibility in one case.

That said, Berlin also has a more general and fairly well documented problem with arson and vandalism targeting cars, with an average of roughly two a night being set alight in the capital city over recent years. Vandalism and insurance fraud are the most common reasons more generally.

Reichelt was fired from his prominent job at Bild in 2021 amid allegations of sexual harassment, accusations he always denied and referred to as a "smear campaign."

Lawmakers in the Bundestag have approved reforms that will provide additional powers to Germany's domestic and external intelligence agencies.

The changes will strengthen both the external Federal Intelligence Service (BND) and domestic intelligence service the BfV, formally titled the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution.

The law passed fairly comfortably in the federal Bundestag lower house of parliament, with 309 votes in favor, 190 against and 71 abstentions.

The BfV will be granted powers beyond intelligence gathering and monitoring individuals, such as being able to secretly enter homes or take action against explosives or weapons.

In the case of the BND, it will be granted additional operational intervention powers, for instance moving to disable servers belonging to state-sponsored hacker groups abroad.

The changes aim to respond to intensified and evolving threats from foreign intelligence services and their partners, and to reduce dependency on information supplied by friendly foreign intelligence services.

Opposition parties have accused the government of abolishing or weakening the separation between the police and intelligence services — a sensitive and closely monitored distinction in German society, because of the legacy both of Adolf Hitler's Nazi regime and of the secret police services in Communist East Germany during the Cold War.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Friedrich Merz has said during his visit to Dublin that Germany and Europe's position in future peace talks for Ukraine is "set."

Following the talks in Abu Dhabi this week between Ukraine and Russia brokered by the US, which also involved European representatives at times, Merz said further negotiations were now planned.

"In the coming weeks there should now be concrete peace talks in which Europe is represented," Merz told reporters in Dublin amid an informal meeting of EU leaders.

He said that "provisionally" this might involve the same "group of Europeans" who had participated in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday and Wednesday.

"Germany is set in there, that is completely clear," he said.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz's call to link EU budget negotiations to the provision of assistance to Ukraine, which faced hefty criticism at home, has found some backing amid European Political Community meetings and an AI summit in Dublin.

Merz, who has been leading the charge to find savings in the next EU budget, said doing so could ensure stronger contributions to helping Ukraine from all EU member states.

Estonia's Prime Minister Kristen Michal said during the meeting in Dublin that he approved of Merz's suggestion "that support for Ukraine is also a part of our core security and our core financing."

He said that members who wanted a new EU budget should contribute.

Latvia's Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs, meanwhile, said he agreed completely with Merz.

"We must all pull in the same direction. All of Europe must do its part," he said.

Luxembourg's Luc Frieden also said that "we must all stand behind Ukraine" and added that collective financial commitments should be a part of this.

As the largest economy and most populous country in the EU, Germany is the largest overall contributor both to the EU budget and to assistance for Ukraine.

Countries that tend to be so-called net beneficiaries of the EU budget, rather than net contributors to it, tend to be more reticent to cut spending plans.

Hosts Ireland, in a tricky position as the holders of the rotating presidency of the EU trying to broker a deal on the next seven-year budget, said it had concerns about adding an additional factor to the stalled talks, as the current budget's expiry at the end of 2027 starts to draw near.

"But I do understand why this is happening," Taoiseach (or prime minister) Micheal Martin said in Dublin. "Some countries have made considerable contributions and they want all EU member states to contribute financially to the support for Ukraine."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The right-wing populist Alternative for Germany (AfD) was critical of both the spending and the fundraising plans in the 2027 budget, claiming without showing its workings that it would be able to do more with less by making swingeing cuts in various key areas.

Budget policy spokesman Michael Espendiller said the budget meant "more debts and more taxes and more burdens for the taxpayer."

He accused the Christian Democrats of breaking key election pledges by raising taxes on alcohol and tobacco. He then complained that despite this, there was not enough money for the promised electricity tax cut.

"If you put it into figures, the federal government will be taking out almost €400,000 (around $440,000) every minute in new debt," Espendiller said, calling for an end to what he called a spiral of debt.

He claimed that the AfD would have able to complete its budget with new debt of just €63 billion, not roughly €210 billion, while simultaneously providing tax relief of around €44 billion.

Espendiller said this would be achieved with wide-reaching cuts in several core areas of spending: climate protection, contributing to the EU budget and other EU funding, asylum-related spending, international development aid, and weapons deliveries and other assistance to Ukraine.

It's unclear to what extent these proposed cuts would be feasible or legal, or what domestic or international implications they might have, or whether they'd save anything like the amount the AfD asserts in practice.

Politicians on the Bundestag budget committee burned the proverbial candle at both ends heading into Friday morning, trying to finalize details of the federal government's spending plans for 2027 before the year's end.

The session took over 15 hours, and already politicians are talking about areas where they still see room for further improvement or alteration — but the document does at least stand in such a form in which it can take effect without too many complications.

Including all spending plans, in the core budget and from the so-called "special funds" for infrastructure and military modernization, new debt constitutes around a third of oultays.

In total, the plan is to take out new debt worth just over €210 billion ($233 billion), while taking in a little less than €400 billion in taxes.

That's the second-highest level of new debt in the post-war history of the Federal Republic of Germany. Even at the height of the COVID pandemic in 2021, new debt was only slightly higher, at €215.4 billion.

We'll likely be returning to the various details of and reactions to this story throughout the morning.

The environmentalist Greens took aim at Chancellor Merz for not delivering on a promise to reduce taxes on electricity in the final budget.

"The big promise that Chancellor Merz made a few days ago, sinking electricity taxes for everyone, this promise remains a broken promise," party co-leader Britta Hasselmann said on ZDF television on Friday.

"It was possible to find a way at short notice for several other things in this budget," she said.

"I think this demonstrates the inadequate planning and the weak leadership of the chancellor," Hasselmann said.

She added that the CDU forcing a delay to the planned sugar tax at short notice was further evidence of the planning shortcomings.

A budget expert at the party, Sebastian Schäfer, similarly alleged a "leadership vacuum in this coalition government," saying that what was put forward was less a budget and more a "wooden shack wihtout foundations."

The Left Party's budget policy spokesman Dietmar Bartsch has lamented a "knot garden of debt, tricks and delays," accusing the coalition of not conducting "responsible budgetary policy."

Despite criticizing the debt levels, Bartsch also said it was "deeply unserious" to float electricity tax relief but then withdraw the plan.

He said this would have cost less money than the federal government's plan to buy a share of the arms company KNDS. He also said it was unacceptable for the center-left Social Democrats to be celebrating just because "the odd welfare cut is not happening."

Ines Schwerdtner, co-leader of the party that firmly opposes defense spending and is at best lukewarm on NATO membership, said the record spending showed that money was not as tight as Merz's government made out.

"The debt brake is suspended for weapons, but for housing and electricity taxes they scrimp for every euro," Schwerdtner said. "The money is there, this government is just distributing it completely incorrectly."

Schwerdtner, herself a member of the budget committed in the Bundestag, called it a "budget of naivete."

More on this morning's top story in Berlin, the 2027 budget being signed off.

As the CDU calls for further savings, the Social Democrats say that the energy tax relief recently touted by Chancellor Friedrich Merz "would have to be financed with additional debts."

Ahead of Thursday's marathon talks, Merz had said he hoped to introduce the tax relief amid the stress caused by issues including the wars in Iran and Ukraine.

The SPD's Dirk Wiese said the junior coalition partners were "not disinclined to pave the way for the electricity tax relief," but not by making cuts elsewhere.

Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil of the SPD had said he did not see enough fiscal wiggle room to enable the desired tax break.

Bremen's mayor Andreas Bovenshulte, also a Social Democrat, said that while he would have welcomed the relief, other decisions meant it wasn't possible.

"For that, a serious financing source would have been required, for instance with a plastic or sugar of windfall tax," Bovenschulte said, in reference to either delayed or proposed but rejected plans to potentially increase tax revenues.

German defense industry startup Quantum Systems said its drones were operational worldwide once again, including with the Bundeswehr military, after a cyberattack by "hostile actors" last month.

The company had announced the cyberattack on Thursday, amid reporting from the Financial Times that also said the Bundeswehr had grounded its drones from the company.

"The fleet is operating normally around the globe — including Germany and the Bundeswehr," a Quantum Systems spokesperson said in an emailed statement to the Reuters news agency. "The Bundeswehr was the only customer to ground their systems as a precaution."

The company, based near Munich, had earlier said it uncovered an "active cyberattack" by hostile actors.

"The threat was contained thanks to the swift response of our IT and security teams in close and transparent collaboration with the authorities," it said in a statement, adding there was no risk for end users and operators using its unmanned systems.

Quantum drones are used by Ukrainian armed forces in their defensive war against Russia, among others.

"Companies at the forefront of supporting Ukraine are being targeted precisely because our work is critically relevant to customers' security," the company said. "Being aware of this responsibility, Quantum Systems has mitigation plans in place and strives to fulfil the highest standard of data and system security."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Senior Christian Democrat Union (CDU) politician Matthias Middelberg appeared on ZDF television this morning to discuss the budget breakthrough.

He identified one "weak point" after the overnight negotiations.

"We have not yet saved enough, we still need to save a lot more," he said.

Middelberg said that in his view the government would not be able to "collect the funds," because that would put too much tax strain on people and businesses.

Therefore, he said, "the government must make cutbacks."

Middelberg acepted that it wasn't clear how to do this, speculating that "perhaps there are subsidies or some other things" that could be ripe to be trimmed.

He said the leadership of the coalition government's CDU/CSU and Social Democrats would "consider this question very closely once more."

The German government statistics agency Destatis has published new figures on insolvency filings for the month of August.

A total of 2,067 companies registered insolvencies with German courts during the month, Destatis said, 4.4% more than in the same month in 2025.

The data operates on something of a delay, because the government tracks when courts grant the status, which can be almost three months after the initial application at times.

The increase has been a rolling trend this year. From January to August, 17,252 companies have filed for insolvency, 6.6% more than in the same period last year.

However, the total sum of debts forgiven in insolvency proceedings is actually quite considerably lower than in the first eight months of last year, at €25.9 billion ($28.7 billion) rather than €37.2 billion, because fewer large companies have gone bust.

More individuals are also filing for bankruptcy protection than in 2025, although the rise is somewhat less sharp. In August, 6,301 people gained insolvency protection, 2.8% more than last August. For January through August, the year-on-year increase is more modest, at 1.2%.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Politicians on the Bundestag budget committee burned the proverbial candle at both ends heading into Friday morning, trying to finalize details of the federal government's spending plans for 2027 before the year's end.

Moin! Here's hoping you slept more and better than the Bundestag's budget committee. Or if not, at least let's hope that you had more fun.

Its members worked towards the dawn in a session lasting over 15 hours, trying to iron out the last wrinkles in spending plans for 2027.

The proverbial white smoke emerged at around 6 in the morning in Berlin, with word of a finalized agreement.

If you were tired of talk and criticism of the "debt brake" and the "black zero" (a promise not to take any new debts) in the years following the eurozone debt crisis, rest assured we can assign such chatter to the history books for now.

The borrowing plans for 2027 — if you incorporate new debt taken out as part of so-called "special funds," for instance for the military and infrastructure, rather than as part of the core budget — are the second highest in the history of post-war Germany.

The country only took out more new debt in 2021, at the height of the COVID pandemic and even then it was very close indeed.

We'll bring you more news and reactions on this, and whatever else breaks around the country, as Friday develops.

#760. Three years on NI Women finally have friendlies again

Northern Ireland's friendly double-header against Greece will be live on BBC iPlayer and BBC Sport website

Tuesday, 18 July 2023 was the last time Northern Ireland Women played a friendly.

Under interim manager Gail Redmond, NI produced a fine display to beat Czech Republic 2-0 in Opava.

Just over three and a half years later, Northern Ireland will have not one but two friendly fixtures, with Michael McArdle's side taking on Greece in an Inver Park double-header on 27 November and 1 December.

A lot has changed for NI since that last friendly, but, having two pressure-free games finally offers McArdle an opportunity to experiment with tactics and personnel as they take the first step towards building for Euro 2029 qualifying.

Magill returns to NI squad for Greece friendlies

Greece were beaten by England in the first round of the World Cup play-offs

Only eight players who were in the squad for that friendly win are in the current crop over three years on.

Rebecca McKenna, Rebecca Holloway and Simone Magill started while Lauren Wade, Kerry Beattie and Joely Andrews came off the bench.

Fi Morgan and Chloe McCarron were unused substitutes.

Goalkeeper Lilie Woods made her debut, Marissa Callaghan captained the side and Sarah McFadden and Beattie scored the goals in a rare away win.

A month after that friendly victory, Tanya Oxtoby arrived to take over as Kenny Shiels' permanent successor.

She eventually left to take over at Newcastle United in November 2025 and all 26 of her games as NI manager were competitive fixtures.

The introduction of the Nations League and its close ties to Euro and World Cup qualification admittedly left little room in what is now a stacked international women's calendar for friendly games.

During Oxtoby's tenure, NI had two Nations League campaigns sandwiched between Euro 2025 qualifiers.

After falling to Iceland in their Nations League promotion/relegation play off last October, they opted against seeking any friendlies at the end of November as they looked for a successor to Oxtoby.

The competitive games kept coming and Kris Lindsay was then in interim charge of NI's first two 2027 World Cup qualifiers before McArdle took over in April for the four remaining group games and the subsequent first-round play-off defeat against Portugal.

With NI not involved in the second round of the World Cup play-offs while many others are in the upcoming window, McArdle has decided to get the squad together for two friendlies.

With such a young squad at his disposal and with McArdle still relatively new to the job, he is relishing the chance to have the players in camp for an extended period and for NI to test themselves against decent opposition.

"We don't want friendly games in this window, we want to be in the play-offs but we had planned for both [scenarios], this has been a long-term plan," he said.

"Greece I specifically selected because I knew we couldn't draw them in the Nations League as we're in the same pot, but also they're a strong nation who are progressing well and are close to ourselves in the rankings.

"They'll be a real test for us. It was very deliberate selection."

Northern Ireland suffered a 7-1 aggregate defeat in the first round World Cup play-off against Portugal

McArdle wants NI to be "more horrible to play against" and feels they will work on that in this camp as well as what they do when in possession to trouble opponents.

Greece, like Northern Ireland, exited the World Cup play-offs at the first round after an aggregate 8-1 defeat to England.

They had been in good form before back-to-back defeats by the Lionesses, winning five games this year as they topped Group C4 to seal promotion to League B.

"It gives us two games to try and win first and foremost because we need to develop the winning mentality, but also to test some things because a lot of the identity and how we play, after six competitive games, there is still work to do particularly in possession, we've not quite done that yet," McArdle continued.

"That identity that we never give up and are constantly going, that is the case for the group, but we have to improve the athleticism and the duels to bridge the gap to qualification to tournaments."

Qualifying for the 2029 Euros in Germany does not begin until 2028, but McArdle's side have a testing Nations League campaign to prepare for next year.

They have been drawn against Poland, Finland and Belarus and the Scot revealed that he is already planning ahead for potential friendly opponents for next year's November/December international window to maximise time spent with his squad if they are not in the Nations League play-offs.

"There's also the importance of taking all the activity available to us and that's crucial for us growing and moving forward.

"We're already planning for next November/December window and selecting opponents because there is a deliberate strategy how we evolve the group.

"Part of that is strategically picking opponents which will help us grow. The friendlies, in a sense it's not competitive games, but we'll approach them in the same way."

Kim Zolciak's daughter tied the knot with Billy Seidl in a beachside ceremony on Nov. 21, nearly three years after announcing their engagement.

Alongside the Instagram video posted the same day of Brielle, 29—whose adoptive dad is Kroy Biermann—and the former baseball player sharing a sweet kiss by the ocean, she wrote with a white heart emoji, "Mrs. Seidl."

She was a blushing bride in white as she walked down the aisle in a strapless ball gown with a tulle skirt and a large black bow adorning her waist, accessorized with a matching white veil. For Billy's part, he said "I do" in a classic black tux.

Brielle's younger sister Ariana Biermann, 25, wasn't tardy to the party, commenting under the announcement, "I'm crying. I love you so much."

Gia Guidice—who stars on Next Gen NYC with Ariana—also celebrated the nuptials IRL and online, writing, "Beautiful [red heart emoji] so so stunning!! so happy for you both."

Meanwhile, Kim shared the clip to her Instagram Stories after the milestone, celebrating her eldest tying the knot.

But as Brielle embraces her new era with Billy, the ongoing sexual assault case against her 15-year-old brother Kroy "KJ" Biermann Jr. has been a shadow over the family.

The teen—who pleaded not guilty to assaulting a 15-year-old in a Lifetime Fitness changing room—was indicted Sept. 3 on seven counts, including aggravated child molestation, aggravated sexual battery, aggravated sodomy, sexual battery against a child under 16 and false imprisonment.

His then-attorney Jason Sheffield (replaced by Bryan Steel earlier this month) argued that as the case moves forward, KJ's innocence will be proven.

"I respect the difficult responsibilities carried by prosecutors and victim advocates," Sheffield wrote in a September statement to E! News. "Cases involving children require patience, care and a commitment from all of us to understanding the full picture as the process continues."

Kim—also mom to 12-year-old twins with Kroy—threw her support behind KJ after his August arrest, describing the allegations against him as "nothing short of reckless and deeply troubling" in a September statement to E! News.

"False accusations can have devastating consequences not only for the person being accused, but also for genuine survivors of sexual assault and abuse," the statement read. "Every legitimate allegation deserves to be taken seriously and investigated based on the facts and evidence. At the same time, no one should be publicly condemned based solely on an accusation."

But the allegations against KJ didn't end with the 15-year-old girl. As prosecutors sought to block the transfer of his April case to juvenile court, they shared insight into 16 previous offenses against the teen from a separate 2025 sexual assault case, according to court documents obtained by E! News.

KJ—whose attorney denied the allegations on his behalf—was charged with incest, eight counts of child molestation, sexual battery, statutory rape and five counts of the sexual exploitation of children in April 2025 after the Milton County Police Department discovered "videos and photos" in a hidden folder on his phone.

Sheffield accused the prosecutors in the case—which is currently with the Fulton County Juvenile Court—of "grossly" misrepresenting the facts in a separate September statement to E! News, adding that the "matter arose from inappropriate, crude behavior involving two middle-schoolers."

#757. The red card that changed Liverpool-Man Utd: correct call?

Ngumoha stars as Liverpool thrash 10-man Man Utd

Leny Yoro's eighth-minute red card was a pivotal moment early in Mauricio Pochettino's first game as Manchester United boss.

It handed Liverpool the initiative at Anfield, and Andoni Iraola's players took advantage by scoring two goals in quick succession.

Was there a case for the video assistant referee (VAR) to suggest it should be downgraded to a yellow?

Let's take a look at the incident, and what a referee takes into account before showing a red for denying an obvious goalscoring opportunity.

Photographers at Anfield captured the sequence of events - from challenge to red card

Photographers at Anfield captured the sequence of events - from challenge to red card

Photographers at Anfield captured the sequence of events - from challenge to red card

Photographers at Anfield captured the sequence of events - from challenge to red card

Photographers at Anfield captured the sequence of events - from challenge to red card

Ronald Araujo played a long ball upfield for Alexander Isak to run on to.

Isak took a touch, before Yoro bundled into the back of the Sweden international and brought him down.

Referee Sam Barrott did not hesitate, giving the foul and sending off Yoro.

Was there doubt that Isak would have taken control of the ball? If so, it should only be a caution.

There are four key considerations for denying an obvious goalscoring opportunity:

distance between the offence and the goal

likelihood of keeping or gaining control of the ball

location and number of defenders and attackers

As Isak was running directly towards goal in a central position, and there was no covering defender, three of the factors were satisfied.

The question is about the "likelihood of keeping or gaining control of the ball".

The Liverpool striker took a heavy touch, which moved the ball a few yards ahead of him.

The touch came before contact from Yoro, so there is no case that the challenge caused Isak to over-run the ball.

The referee and the VAR, John Brooks, must therefore assess whether Isak would definitely have got to the ball ahead of Senne Lammens. And that if he had, it would have been a good scoring chance.

If there is any doubt, then it should not be a red card.

It is a borderline case, and as such the VAR would not be expected to intervene for a clear and obvious error.

Likewise, if the referee had shown a yellow the VAR would not get involved.

Former Liverpool and England midfielder Danny Murphy, who is a pundit on Sunday's Match of the Day, said there was "no doubt" about the red card.

Former Manchester United defender Gary Neville also agreed with the decision.

"Leny Yoro has to cover and he doesn't," Neville said on Sky Sports. "He reacts late and his anticipation is poor.

"It's so clumsy from Yoro. It's naivety, he just needs to get off the pitch. You're not going to get that turned around, no chance."

But for Liverpool boss Iraola the decision is not up for debate.

"I think he's the last man, no?" he said. "It's a clear foul and a red card, yes?

Did Liverpool 'get lucky' with red card decision?

Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes felt it should not have been a red card and said the decision had a detrimental impact on the game.

"It's one that needs to be looked at," Fernandes told Sky Sports.

"We have far too many meetings with the referees for this to happen to us again. The last one against Chelsea [when Lisandro Martinez was sent off], you can give it as a red card and it was probably a second yellow also. Today, you can't give a red card.

"It's very clear they show us if the player is not in control of the ball, it's never a red card.

"Isak kicks the ball forward, the ball goes into the hands of Senne. Isak has got no control of the ball, he has no chance to get on the ball. He puts his leg across to try to get some advantage from Leny. I can understand the fall, but it's never a red card.

"There are too many referees on the pitch and too many on VAR taking so long to see to make a mistake like this that can change the game.

"It's not because of them we conceded the goal from the free-kick, but it changes the game completely."

Pochettino, meanwhile, was frustrated by what he perceived as inconsistency in the decision-making of the officials.

The former Tottenham and Chelsea boss felt his new team should have been awarded a penalty moments before Yoro was sent off, after Jeremy Jacquet went shoulder to shoulder with Bryan Mbeumo.

"It's difficult to accept that because it was a foul under my view and for me was a penalty," Pochettino told Match of the Day.

"Look how everything changes if that action was a red card and a foul, I think we need to review. When I played football that situation is normal. The action against Mbeumo, if that [Yoro foul on Isak] was a red card then that was a penalty."

'We have too many referees' - Fernandes disagrees with Yoro red

There have been a couple of very similar cases this season.

Brighton's Pascal Struijk was sent off at Sunderland through a VAR review after he brought down Wilson Isidor.

The Seagulls successfully appealed against that red card on the grounds that there was clear doubt that Isidor would have taken control of the ball before it ran through to goalkeeper Bart Verbruggen.

Could Manchester United appeal against Yoro's red card? There's nothing to lose by doing so.

Despite the Football Association regulatory commission unanimously ruling the Struijk red card was wrong, the Premier League's key match incidents panel voted the VAR intervention was a correct call on a split 3-2 vote.

Ipswich's Issa Diop avoided a VAR red card for a foul on James McAtee against Nottingham Forest, when the referee disagreed with the video official, and believed there was a covering defender. Forest boss Oliver Glasner was adamant it had been a clear goalscoring opportunity.

It was the same referee, Thomas Bramall, for both of those incidents.

That shows just how subjective such decisions can be. It is often rare to get a real consensus.

Yoro can count himself a little unfortunate to get the red card.

#756. Christine Brown Shares How Granddad’s Murder Shaped Polygamous Beliefs

Sister Wives’ Christine Brown shared how her grandfather Rulon Clark Allred’s 1977 assassination inspired her polygamous marriage to ex-husband Kody Brown: “They shot him, they gunned him down.”

Christine Brown is shedding light on a dark chapter in her family history.

The Sister Wives star—who announced she was leaving her plural marriage to Kody Brown in 2021—detailed how the life and tragic death of her grandfather Rulon Clark Allred impacted her views around polygamy.

“The biggest reason I wanted to live a plural marriage was because of my grandmas,” Christine told husband David Woolley during the Nov. 22 episode of Sister Wives. “My grandpa was killed when I was 5 and my grandmas were still best friends after that.”

“And they stayed together and they hung out together all the time,” she added. “So I thought that would be an ideal situation.”

Before his death in 1977, Rulon had an integral role in his community as the leader of the Apostolic United Brethren fundamentalist group in Utah.

And throughout his time as a religious leader, the TLC star noted that her grandfather “believed in being public” and thought it was “really important to open up and let people know” about his family life.

But not everyone was pleased with his teachings.

“He had this article where he talked about how he believed he was a prophet, he was the mouthpiece for God on this planet. And there was someone else from another church and he felt like he was actually the mouthpiece for God,” she said. “He got his wives to kill my grandpa. Right there at work, in front of one of his wives. It was terrible. They shot him, they gunned him down.”

In 1980, a court convicted Ervil LeBaron for criminal homicide for ordering Allred's death. He was sentenced to life in prison.

Today, the 54-year-old—who shares six kids with Kody—still thinks of the moment she learned of her grandfather’s assassination as “one of my pivotal memories.”

“I just remember, starkly, the sadness of my dad but being so sad at such a loss because he was cool,” she explained. “My grandpa was super cool. No one ever said a negative word about my grandpa. No one. Everyone loved him.”

And it was his example that prompted the reality TV star to enter what would be a 30-year spiritual marriage with Kody alongside his wives Meri Brown, Janelle Brown and Robyn Brown. (Janelle separated from Kody in 2022 while Meri also split from their relationship in 2024.)

“I don’t know what’s different, I have no idea,” Christine shared. “My parents were polygamists, married into polygamy. I believed in it so much and I saw the potential of how good it could be [from] my grandmas, with my grandpa.”

That’s why she ultimately “followed in their footsteps a bit.”

Keep reading for a closer look into Christine’s family…

Born May 21, 1994, Logan is the oldest son of Kody Brown and Janelle Brown. He is also the eldest child of 18 in Kody's entire brood.

After graduating with a master's degree in business administration from the University of Nevada in 2020, he married Michelle Petty two years later.

Aspyn is the oldest child of Kody and Christine Brown. She was born on March 14, 1995.

Also a University of Nevada alum, Aspyn tied the knot with Mitch Thompson in 2018. She announced her pregnancy in April 2025.

Born on July 29, 1995, Leon is the only child of Kody and Meri Brown.

In 2020, Leon came out as transgender, sharing that they were previously "socialized as a girl."

"I was pretty young & unfortunately i grew up in a context that was incredibly gendered & restrictive," Leon—who also goes by "Leo"—wrote on Instagram. "and here’s the thing, i’m finally ready to share my favorite self with the world. and that self is incredibly genderqueer, trans, and unapologetic."

#755. Morocco and Senegal await Afcon final verdict after court case

Sadio Mane was named best player at the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations

Everyone knows a football match should take 90 minutes, but the final of the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations has been playing out for 10 months.

Now, finally, Morocco or Senegal will be crowned winners. However, that moment of glory will come in a courtroom, not on the pitch.

On Tuesday afternoon sport's highest legal authority, the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas), will render its judgement on Senegal's appeal against the decision to strip them of the title they thought they won in January against the hosts in Rabat.

The case was heard in early October, and the wait is almost over.

With 66,000 fans creating an electric atmosphere in the Prince Moulay Abdellah Stadium, Morocco were chasing their first Afcon title since 1976.

But the final descended into chaos deep into second-half stoppage time.

With the match goalless, Senegal thought Ismaila Sarr had scored a dramatic winner, only to discover that referee Jean Jacques Ndala had blown for a Morocco free-kick.

The controversy deepened in the 98th minute when, after a video assistant referee (VAR) review, Ndala awarded Morocco a penalty.

Tempers boiled over on the touchline and in the stands. Senegal coach Pape Thiaw led some of his players and staff down the tunnel, while supporters clashed with security as order briefly collapsed.

Play eventually resumed and, in the 124th minute, Morocco missed a golden chance to end their 50-year wait for continental glory when Brahim Diaz failed to convert a penalty, chipping it 'Panenka' style into the arms of goalkeeper Edouard Mendy.

Pape Gueye's extra-time strike then secured a 1-0 win for Senegal, who lifted the trophy for a second time.

The Royal Moroccan Football Federation (FMRF) quickly lodged a complaint with the Confederation of African Football (Caf), arguing that Senegal had breached competition regulations.

Article 82, contained within a chapter titled 'Withdrawals', states: "If, for any reason whatsoever, a team... refuses to play or leaves the ground before the regular end of the match without the authorisation of the referee", they shall be "considered [the loser] and shall be eliminated from the current competition".

In March a Caf appeals board agreed, ruling that Senegal had forfeited the match and awarding Morocco a 3-0 victory.

While there is precedent for Caf overturning results during Afcon and World Cup qualifying, some people, including one former senior Caf official, argued that only the referee has the authority to abandon a match if a walk-off occurs.

The FMRF said it was seeking the proper application of tournament regulations, but Senegal's federation (FSF) described the ruling as "unfair, unprecedented and unacceptable" and appealed to Cas.

Some Senegal supporters were initially convicted of hooliganism offences after clashes during the final but eventually returned home after receiving a royal pardon

Founded in 1984 and based in the Swiss city of Lausanne, Cas was set up as an independent legal body designed to settle disputes as global sport became more lucrative and, as a result, more litigious.

For governing bodies which recognise Cas' authority, it is deemed to be the supreme arbiter, meaning its ruling is final unless, in rare cases, Switzerland's highest court decides to set it aside based on a limited number of technicalities.

More than 900 cases are filed every year, from more than 50 different sports, covering issues such as employment contracts and transfers, doping, corruption, TV rights and, in this case, the organisation of sporting events.

The FSF's appeal was heard in private on 8 October by a panel of three arbitrators chosen by Cas for their expertise in sports law.

The panel was led by Frenchman Gerald Simon, founder of the Sports Law Laboratory at the University of Burgundy and a Cas member for 23 years.

Italian international law professor Luigi Fumagalli and Hamburg-based attorney and professor of âlaw at the University of Zurich Ulrich Haas completed the trio.

If the panel had failed to come to a consensus on the case, Cas president Simon will have made the final decision.

Although Caf's appeals board is independent, a reversal of its judgement would deliver another blow to the reputation of African football's governing body, which has been heavily criticised for the retrospective decision to hand Morocco the title.

Caf president Patrice Motsepe said in March that it will "adhere to" and "respect" whatever Cas decides, so, if things go in Senegal's favour, it could mean someone having to tinker with the Afcon rulebook.

The Senegal walk-off has, however, already brought about a change in football's rules.

"The referee may sanction with a red card any player who leaves the field of play in protest at â a âreferee's decision," said Ifab, the game's lawmaking body, in April.

"This new rule will also apply âto any team official who incites players to leave the field of play. A team that causes a match âto be abandoned will, in principle, forfeit the match."

Thiaw lost his job following Senegal's last-32 World Cup exit this summer, while Walid Regragui, the man in the Morocco dugout in January, was dismissed in March.

Whatever the outcome of the case, animosity is likely to linger between the two federations.

The FMRF's senior hierarchy was furious with Senegal's behaviour, believing the pictures beamed around the world irrevocably tarnished the image of the first Afcon hosted by the kingdom since 1988 - a tournament into which a huge amount of time and money had been invested.

The FSF and the Senegalese government have leaned into a feeling prevalent across the continent that Morocco holds too much influence within African football.

Other incidents also irked Senegal, such as laser pens being directed into players' eyes and ball boys moving goalkeeper Mendy's towel, something which led to the barely believable sight of reserve keeper Yehvann Diouf being tackled to the ground by three ball boys when he tried to intervene.

With the next Afcon scheduled to take place in June and July next year, the chances of a high-profile rematch between Africa's best two teams is a tantalising thought.

While the chaos of this year's final may have given birth to a new rivalry for fans to revel in, there is unanimous agreement that such encounters should be settled on the pitch and not in a courtroom.

#754. Germany's Nmecha won't repeat controversial goal celebration

Germany head coach Jürgen Klopp has said midfielder Felix Nmecha will not repeat a goal celebration that sparked controversy over the past week. Germany are set to face Serbia and the Netherlands in the Nations League.

With the controversy sparked by Felix Nmecha's celebrations after his goals in Dortmund's 2-1 win over Elfersberg last weekend, the subject was always going to be top of reporters' minds when Germany coach Jürgen Klopp faced reporters ahead of Friday's match against Serbia.

Nmecha celebrated the goals by mimicking taking a crown off his head and kneeling to place it on the ground.

This was understood by many to be a nod to a Ballers in God (BIG) campaign called "The King's Return."

BIG, a Christian group for footballers, has said it aims to "demonstrate love and respect towards everyone," but critics claim it discriminates against the queer and transexual people. The discourse generated by the celebration did not go unnoticed by the Germany boss.

​Klopp told reporters in Belgrade on Thursday evening, that the 26-year-old Nmecha had assured him that he meant no harm by his actions.

"Last weekend I ​saw Felix score two great goals and saw the celebration and then the gesture. I thought nothing of it at the time, but then it all kicked off," he said.

"As the controversy escalated, I started looking into the details of the subject and trying to form a clear picture of it.

"I confronted him with all the things you (reporters) might have confronted him with. He told me that it had nothing to do with that at all, and that he loves all people and does not discriminate against anyone."

He then said that Nmecha had agreed not to repeat the celebration.

In Friday's match, Klopp's goal will be to keep alive Germany's chances of reaching the Nations League quarterfinals with a win over Serbia. Germany are third in Group A2 with 5 points, trailing the Netherlands and Greece, who both have 8. Serbia, who Germany beat 2-0 in Munich last month, are still without a win.

"We feel well prepared," Klopp said, adding that his team were committed to earning "a final" for the last group last group game on Monday in Berlin against the Netherlands.

Klopp also expressed his disappointment that only a few thousand Serbian children would be admitted to the stadium due to a spectator ban. Originally, the game was to be played behind closed doors after Serbia was sanctioned for racist and discriminatory behavior by its fans. However, a clause in the UEFA rules allows a selected group of guests to attend. Now children under 15 accompanied by teachers or football coaches are expected to be at the match.

"We're expecting some 5,000 guests," a spokesman for the Serbian FA told the DPA news agency. The stadium's capacity is 55,000. The German FA has been allocated just 50 tickets for its fans.
